messages.content: Our growth review keeps quoting an 'activation rate' but nobody can tell me exactly what it counts. Can you pin the definition down as a query on our signups table - who is in the numerator, who is in the denominator, and what gets excluded?

A KPI nobody can reproduce is a rumor, so here is the definition written as queries you can rerun. Signups carry a flag for activation within 7 days of signup, and test accounts are excluded from both sides of the fraction - an exclusion that applies to the denominator matters as much as one that applies to the numerator:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE signups (user_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, signup_date TEXT NOT NULL, activated_within_7d INTEGER NOT NULL, is_test INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS activated FROM signups WHERE is_test = 0 AND activated_within_7d = 1
SELECT COUNT(*) AS eligible_signups FROM signups WHERE is_test = 0

messages.content: Activation rate for March, by the definition above: 6 activated out of 10 eligible signups = 60%. The definition, in words: of all non-test accounts created in the window, the share that reached the activation event within 7 days of signup. Three choices in it deserve to be written next to the number wherever it is quoted. First, the 7-day window: a user who activates on day 9 counts as not activated, which is a product judgment, not a fact. Second, the test-account exclusion removes the internal traffic - 2 of the 12 signups here - from both numerator and denominator; leave them in and the rate reads differently while describing nothing real. Third, the denominator is signups in the window, not active users or sessions. Anyone quoting a different activation rate is using a different definition, and the honest response is to ask for their numerator and denominator, not to argue about whose number is bigger.
Finance says our churn hit 72% last month and the success team says it was 25%. Same month, same accounts table. Can you reconcile the two numbers and show me exactly where they diverge?

Both teams are computing a real quantity - they are just not computing the same one. The accounts table carries each account's starting monthly revenue in cents and a churn flag, so I can run both definitions side by side:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE accounts (account TEXT PRIMARY KEY, mrr_start_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, churned INTEGER NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('Northwind', 120000, 0), ('Alder', 45000, 0), ('Beacon', 980000, 1), ('Corvus', 30000, 0), ('Delta Labs', 62000, 0), ('Ember', 27000, 1), ('Fjord', 84000, 0), ('Gale', 51000, 0)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_accounts, SUM(churned) AS churned_accounts FROM accounts
SELECT SUM(mrr_start_cents) AS total_mrr, SUM(CASE WHEN churned = 1 THEN mrr_start_cents ELSE 0 END) AS churned_mrr FROM accounts

messages.content: Reconciled. The success team's 25% is logo churn: 2 churned accounts out of 8 = 25%. Finance's figure is revenue churn: the churned accounts carried 1007000 cents of the 1399000 cents starting MRR = 72%. One account, Beacon, held 980000 of the 1399000 cents and it churned; Ember, the other loss, was only 27000. Logo churn treats those two losses as equals, revenue churn weights them by money, and with a book this concentrated the two definitions can never tell the same story. Neither team made an arithmetic error; the company has been quoting one word for two quantities. Fix the vocabulary in the pack - 'logo churn' and 'revenue churn', both reported - and add a concentration note whenever one account is a large share of the base, because a single Beacon deciding to leave moves revenue churn more than a quarter of small-account losses.

We changed the definition of first response time in January - it used to average every ticket, now it only counts tickets opened on business days. Leadership says support got worse in February. Can you restate the history under the new definition so we are comparing like with like?

Comparing a series across a definition change manufactures a trend that may not exist. The tickets table records each ticket's month, the weekday it was opened (0 = Sunday, 6 = Saturday), and its first response in hours. Here is the series both ways - the old all-ticket mean, and the new business-day-only mean applied backwards:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE tickets (ticket_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, month TEXT NOT NULL, opened_dow INTEGER NOT NULL, resp_hours REAL NOT NULL)
SELECT month, ROUND(AVG(resp_hours), 2) AS old_def_mean FROM tickets GROUP BY month ORDER BY month
SELECT month, ROUND(AVG(resp_hours), 2) AS new_def_mean FROM tickets WHERE opened_dow BETWEEN 1 AND 5 GROUP BY month ORDER BY month

messages.content:
The old-definition series:
month | old_def_mean
2025-11 | 9.25
2025-12 | 9
2026-01 | 8.57
2026-02 | 8.95
The restated series, new definition applied to every month:
month | new_def_mean
2025-11 | 3.5
2025-12 | 4
2026-01 | 3.65
2026-02 | 3.9
Under the old definition February reads 8.95 hours and looks like a collapse from November's 9.25. Under the new definition February is 3.9 hours against November's 3.5 - a mild drift, not a collapse, and January (3.65) sits in line. The 5.05-hour gap between February's two readings is not performance; it is the weekend tickets. Weekend first responses are slow because a skeleton crew covers them, and the old mean silently averaged two different services - a staffed weekday desk and a thin weekend rota - into one number. The rule this teaches: when a definition changes, restate the history under the new definition before anyone discusses the trend, and keep the old series archived and labeled, never overwritten. If leadership also cares about weekend cover, that is a separate KPI worth defining on its own, not a reason to keep the blended one.
Marketing is celebrating: sessions are up 40% this month. I have a sessions and orders table by week. Can you check whether the number that actually drives decisions moved at all?

Sessions are a vanity metric when they never change a decision - they measure that people arrived, not that anything happened. The decision metric on this table is checkout completion: orders per session. Both, by week:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE weekly_metrics (week TEXT PRIMARY KEY, sessions INTEGER NOT NULL, orders INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT ROUND(320 * 100.0 / 10000, 2) AS first_week_pct
SELECT ROUND(361 * 100.0 / 14000, 2) AS last_week_pct

messages.content: Sessions did grow 40% across the four weeks, from 10000 to 14000 - marketing's number is arithmetically true. But checkout completion fell from 3.2% in the first week to 2.58% in the last, and orders grew only 12.8% while traffic grew 40%. The extra 4000 weekly sessions produced 41 extra orders; the funnel got wider at the top and leakier in the middle. This is the vanity/decision distinction in one table: sessions can be bought with spend and will almost always oblige by rising, so they cannot falsify a strategy. Orders per session can fall, which is exactly what makes it useful - it is the number that would change a decision (pause the campaign, fix the landing page, check what changed in the traffic mix). Keep sessions in the pack as context if you like, but the headline belongs to the metric that can embarrass you. A dashboard where every number only goes up is not reporting; it is applause.

Our on-time delivery KPI needs a defensible definition before I put it in the weekly pack. We have a deliveries table with promised and actual dates and a delay-cause flag. Build the definition as queries, please.

The definition that survives arguments is: of deliveries that were ours to control, the share that arrived by the promised date. Delays caused by the customer (not home, changed address) are excluded from the denominator entirely - they are not late deliveries and they are not on-time ones either:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE deliveries (delivery_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, promised_date TEXT NOT NULL, actual_date TEXT, delay_cause TEXT NOT NULL)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS on_time FROM deliveries WHERE delay_cause <> 'customer' AND actual_date <= promised_date
SELECT COUNT(*) AS controllable FROM deliveries WHERE delay_cause <> 'customer'

messages.content: On-time delivery, March sample: 5 on time out of 8 controllable deliveries = 62.5%. The denominator is the definition's whole argument. Ten deliveries were made; two were delayed by the customer, so they leave the fraction entirely rather than counting as failures - counting them would punish the operation for the customer's calendar and, worse, would tempt the team to argue about cause codes instead of fixing carrier and warehouse delays, which are the three genuine misses here (two carrier, one warehouse). Note also what on-time means: actual_date on or before promised_date, with early counting as on time. If the business later wants 'in the promised window' with early penalized for perishables, that is a new version of the KPI, not a tweak - it gets a new effective date and the history gets restated or the series gets a visible break. Write the cause-code list next to the definition; the day someone invents a new cause code, the denominator quietly changes.

Our services lead reports utilization of 81% but she calculates it over contracted hours including vacation. I think the denominator should be hours actually available to work. Can you run both definitions on our consultants table and show the gap?

Utilization is billable hours over some denominator, and the denominator is where the argument lives. The table carries contracted hours, paid time off, and billable hours per consultant for the month, so both versions are one query apart:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE consultants (name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, contracted_hours REAL NOT NULL, pto_hours REAL NOT NULL, billable_hours REAL NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(billable_hours) AS billable, SUM(contracted_hours) AS contracted, SUM(contracted_hours - pto_hours) AS available FROM consultants

messages.content: Billable hours are 536 either way - the numerator is not in dispute. Over contracted hours (760) utilization is 70.5%. Over available hours - contracted minus the 760 hours' worth of PTO, which totals 88 hours across the team, leaving 672 - utilization is 79.8%. Neither is the lead's 81%, which suggests her sheet has a third denominator hiding in it, and that is precisely the problem with an undefined KPI: three honest people produce three numbers. The available-hours version is the one that can steer staffing, because PTO is not capacity the firm failed to sell; the contracted version systematically punishes months with holidays in them and makes December look like a motivation problem. Whichever the firm chooses, the definition record should state the denominator in words next to the KPI name in the pack - 'utilization (of available hours)' - so a reader never has to guess which fraction they are looking at.

For the weekly pack I need a repeat purchase rate. My working definition: of customers whose first order was in the cohort month, the share who placed a second order within 90 days. Can you implement exactly that on our orders table?

Implemented literally as stated - the cohort is defined by the first order's month, and the 90-day window is measured from that first order, not from the calendar month end. The distinction matters and the query makes it visible:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT NOT NULL, order_date TEXT NOT NULL)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS cohort_customers FROM (SELECT customer, MIN(order_date) AS first_order FROM orders GROUP BY customer HAVING strftime('%Y-%m', first_order) = '2026-01')

SELECT COUNT(*) AS repeated FROM (SELECT customer, MIN(order_date) AS first_order FROM orders GROUP BY customer HAVING strftime('%Y-%m', first_order) = '2026-01') c JOIN orders o ON o.customer = c.customer AND o.order_date > c.first_order AND julianday(o.order_date) - julianday(c.first_order) <= 90

messages.content: January cohort repeat rate: 2 of 4 customers ordered again within 90 days = 75%. The four January first-time customers are Ivy, Jay, Kim, and Lou. Ivy repeated at day 46 and Kim at day 55; Jay's second order came at day 139, outside the window, so Jay counts as not repeated even though he did come back - the window is a definition, and Jay is its cost. Lou never returned. Two disciplines this definition needs in the pack. First, the cohort is only measurable 90 days after the month closes, so the January rate could not honestly appear in the pack until the end of April; publishing it earlier means quietly measuring a shorter window for recent cohorts and making the recent past look worse than the distant past. Second, Mel and Ora are February cohort and belong to February's rate, not this one. Repeat rate by cohort month, published on a 90-day lag, is slower than anyone wants - and it is the only version of the number that means the same thing every week.

Support's SLA KPI is 'responded within 4 hours'. The team lead wants tickets that were waiting on the customer excluded from the clock entirely. Can you show what the attainment looks like under both the plain definition and his version?

His version is defensible - a ticket cannot breach a response clock while the ball is in the customer's court - but it changes both the numerator and the denominator, so let us measure both on the same tickets. Response minutes are recorded gross, and minutes waiting on the customer are recorded separately:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE sla_tickets (ticket_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, response_minutes INTEGER NOT NULL, waiting_customer_minutes INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN response_minutes <= 240 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS within_plain, COUNT(*) AS total FROM sla_tickets
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN response_minutes - waiting_customer_minutes <= 240 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS within_adj FROM sla_tickets

messages.content: Plain definition: 5 of 10 tickets responded within 4 hours = 50%. Lead's definition, netting out customer-waiting time: 9 of 10 = 90%. Only ticket 7 breaches under both (700 gross, 200 net - that one is genuinely ours). A 40-point swing from a definitional choice is not a rounding issue; it is the whole KPI. The netted version is the fairer measure of the team's work, and I would adopt it - with two guards written into the definition. First, the waiting minutes must come from status timestamps, not agent estimates, or the exclusion becomes a place to hide breaches. Second, publish the gross figure alongside for one quarter so readers can see the bridge between the old series and the new one. What you must not do is switch silently: a pack that jumps from 50% to 90% with no note teaches readers that the numbers are negotiable, and they will stop believing the honest ones too.

Inventory turnover for the pack: I keep seeing it computed against the ending inventory, but our buyer says it should be against average inventory. Run it both ways on our monthly figures so I can settle it.

Turnover is cost of goods sold divided by the inventory level that supported those sales. Ending inventory is a snapshot that a single delivery can distort; the average of the month's opening and closing balances is the standard denominator. Both, from the same figures (all cents):

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE inventory_month (month TEXT PRIMARY KEY, opening_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, closing_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, cogs_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO inventory_month VALUES ('2026-03', 820000, 610000, 1430000)
SELECT cogs_cents, closing_cents, (opening_cents + closing_cents) / 2 AS avg_cents FROM inventory_month

messages.content: March COGS was 1430000 cents. Against ending inventory (610000 cents) turnover reads 2.34 turns. Against average inventory (715000 cents - the mean of the 820000 opening and 610000 closing balances) it reads 2 turns. The buyer is right, and this month shows why: a large sale late in March drew the closing balance down, so the ending-inventory version credits the business with efficiency that is partly just timing - sell hard on the 30th and any month can look lean. The average denominator is harder to flatter with calendar luck. Whichever the pack adopts, the deeper rule is that the denominator choice belongs in the KPI's definition record, because turnover feeds purchasing decisions: at 2 turns a month the buyer is replenishing roughly every two weeks of cover, and ordering policy built on the flattered 2.34 figure would quietly understock. Same COGS, same shelves - the definition is the decision.

I want a definition registry for our KPIs - a table the dashboard can be held to, with versions. Can you set one up and show me how the current definition of refund rate is retrieved and what a definition change looks like in it?

The registry treats a definition as data: name, version, numerator, denominator, window, exclusions, owner, and the date the version takes effect. A change is a new row, never an edit, so history stays auditable. Here it is with refund rate's two versions and one other KPI:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE kpi_definitions (kpi TEXT NOT NULL, version INTEGER NOT NULL, numerator TEXT NOT NULL, denominator TEXT NOT NULL, window TEXT NOT NULL, exclusions TEXT NOT NULL, owner TEXT NOT NULL, effective_from TEXT NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO kpi_definitions VALUES ('refund_rate', 1, 'refunded order value', 'gross order value', 'calendar month', 'none', 'Priya', '2025-07-01'), ('refund_rate', 2, 'refunded order value', 'gross order value', 'calendar month', 'refunds on orders cancelled before dispatch', 'Priya', '2026-01-01'), ('activation_rate', 1, 'signups activated within 7 days', 'non-test signups', 'calendar month', 'test accounts', 'Marco', '2025-09-01')
SELECT kpi, version, numerator, denominator, window, exclusions, owner, effective_from FROM kpi_definitions WHERE kpi = 'refund_rate' ORDER BY effective_from DESC LIMIT 1

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
kpi | version | numerator | denominator | window | exclusions | owner | effective_from
refund_rate | 2 | refunded order value | gross order value | calendar month | refunds on orders cancelled before dispatch | Priya | 2026-01-01

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS registered_kpis FROM (SELECT DISTINCT kpi FROM kpi_definitions)

messages.content: The current refund rate definition, as the registry returns it: version 2, effective 2026-01-01, owner Priya. Numerator: refunded order value. Denominator: gross order value. Window: calendar month. Exclusions: refunds on orders cancelled before dispatch. Version 2 changed exactly one thing from version 1 - refunds on orders cancelled before dispatch left the numerator - and because the change is a row with an effective date, anyone can reconstruct what the KPI meant in any past month and restate history when a change is meant to apply backwards. The registry currently holds 2 KPIs; every tile on the dashboard should be traceable to one of its rows, and a tile that cannot name its registry row is a number without a contract. Two operating rules make this work: definitions are inserted, never updated in place, and the pack's footnote names the version in force ('refund rate v2') so a reader comparing across the January break knows the series changed definition, not just value.

Build me this week's one-page pack from our daily sales table: headline revenue, orders, and average order value for the week of March 2, each figure traced to a query so I can defend every number in the room.
Every figure on the page comes from the daily table in this session - nothing is typed in from another report. Amounts are cents; the week runs March 2 to March 8:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE daily_sales (day TEXT PRIMARY KEY, orders INTEGER NOT NULL, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(orders) AS orders, SUM(revenue_cents) AS revenue_cents FROM daily_sales
SELECT day, revenue_cents FROM daily_sales ORDER BY revenue_cents DESC LIMIT 1

messages.content: Week of March 2, headline figures: revenue 7404000 cents on 1048 orders, average order value 7065 cents. Saturday March 7 was the peak day at 1539000 cents - nearly a fifth of the week's revenue on one day - and Sunday the trough at 664000, which is the normal shape for this business, not a problem to explain. The discipline on display matters more than the numbers: the three headline figures are one SUM query and one division over a single table, so anyone in the room can be shown the exact rows behind them. A pack figure that arrives from someone's spreadsheet cannot be defended this way, and undefendable figures are the ones that get argued about for twenty minutes. Keep the daily grain in the table even though the pack shows the week - the drill-down from a headline to its days is the first question every pack reader asks, and it should take one query, not a follow-up email.
Revenue is up week over week and the exec team wants to know why. I have orders and revenue for both weeks in a summary table. Can you decompose the change into a volume effect and a rate effect?

Revenue is orders times average order value, so the change splits exactly: the volume effect is the extra orders valued at last week's AOV, and the rate effect is the AOV change applied to this week's orders. The two effects sum to the total change - that identity is the check on the arithmetic:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE week_summary (week TEXT PRIMARY KEY, orders INTEGER NOT NULL, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO week_summary VALUES ('W09', 1000, 6900000), ('W10', 1120, 8064000)
SELECT week, orders, revenue_cents, ROUND(revenue_cents * 1.0 / orders, 0) AS aov_cents FROM week_summary ORDER BY week

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
week | orders | revenue_cents | aov_cents
W09 | 1000 | 6900000 | 6900
W10 | 1120 | 8064000 | 7200

Revenue rose 1164000 cents week over week. The bridge: volume effect 828000 cents - 120 more orders at last week's AOV of 6900 cents. Rate effect 336000 cents - this week's AOV of 7200 cents applied across this week's 1120 orders. The two effects sum exactly to the 1164000 change, which is how you know the decomposition is complete and nothing is hiding in a rounding bucket. The story the bridge tells: roughly 71% of the growth was more orders and 29% was each order being worth more - growth you can believe in differently than pure price growth, because volume growth at a held AOV suggests demand, while pure rate growth on flat volume would suggest the same customers paying more, which has a ceiling. Put the bridge in the pack every week, not just on big weeks. A bridge that only appears when revenue jumps teaches readers to expect an explanation only for good news; the same decomposition on a down week is where it earns its keep.

Something is off: this week's pack shows returns-adjusted revenue, but last week's pack did not exclude returns, and nobody changed the definition on purpose. I have the sales table with a transaction type column. Show me how the pack's own consistency check should have caught this.

The check is simple and should run every week before the pack ships: compute the headline both ways - the pack's standing definition (net of returns) and gross - and require the published figure to match the standing definition exactly. Here is the failure, reproduced:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE sales (txn_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, week TEXT NOT NULL, txn_type TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT week, SUM(amount_cents) AS gross_cents FROM sales GROUP BY week ORDER BY week
SELECT week, SUM(CASE WHEN txn_type = 'sale' THEN amount_cents ELSE 0 END) + SUM(CASE WHEN txn_type = 'return' THEN amount_cents ELSE 0 END) AS net_cents FROM sales GROUP BY week ORDER BY week
SELECT week, SUM(amount_cents) AS returns_cents FROM sales WHERE txn_type = 'return' GROUP BY week ORDER BY week

messages.content:
The gross and net queries return identical rows here because the return rows already carry negative amounts - and that is exactly how the inconsistency slipped through. Gross by week:
week | gross_cents
W10 | 875000
W11 | 901000
Returns by week: W10 -45000 cents, W11 -52000 cents. Last week's pack summed all rows and called it revenue; this week's pack author, trying to be careful, filtered to sales only and published 953000 for W11 against a W10 figure of 875000 that had returns netted inside it - comparing a gross week to a net week and reporting growth that is partly a filter change. The consistency check that catches this class of error: the pack build recomputes every headline from the standing definition query stored with the pack, and separately asserts that this week's build query is byte-identical to last week's. Filters are part of the definition. A well-meaning analyst improving a filter mid-series is a definition change, and definition changes go through the registry with an effective date - or the pack will keep manufacturing trends out of methodology.
Revenue jumped this week and I need the three movers for the pack, with causes, not just totals. Sales are in a table by category. Drill in and tell me what actually moved.
A mover earns its place in the pack by size of change and by having a traced cause. Here is the week-over-week change by category first, then the drill into the biggest one:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE category_sales (category TEXT NOT NULL, week TEXT NOT NULL, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO category_sales VALUES ('Hardware', 'W10', 2100000), ('Hardware', 'W11', 2180000), ('Services', 'W10', 1450000), ('Services', 'W11', 1890000), ('Consumables', 'W10', 980000), ('Consumables', 'W11', 905000), ('Digital', 'W10', 640000), ('Digital', 'W11', 655000)

SELECT category, SUM(CASE WHEN week = 'W11' THEN revenue_cents ELSE -revenue_cents END) AS change_cents FROM category_sales GROUP BY category ORDER BY ABS(SUM(CASE WHEN week = 'W11' THEN revenue_cents ELSE -revenue_cents END)) DESC

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
category | change_cents
Services | 440000
Hardware | 80000
Consumables | -75000
Digital | 15000

arguments.sql: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN week = 'W11' THEN revenue_cents ELSE -revenue_cents END) AS total_change FROM category_sales

messages.content:
Total change: +460000 cents. The movers, by absolute change:
category | change_cents
Services | 440000
Hardware | 80000
Consumables | -75000
Digital | 15000
Mover one is Services, +440000 cents - 95.7% of the entire week's growth. The drill question for Services is whether the jump is one contract or broad demand, and the pack should not print the mover until someone has answered it at the next grain down. Mover two is Consumables, -75000: a decline worth a watch note, not an investigation, at this size. Hardware (+80000) and Digital (+15000) are noise-level and stay off the page. The pack discipline: three movers maximum, each with a cause traced at least one grain deeper than the headline, and each sized against the total change so readers can see whether the story is one category or the whole business. A pack that lists every category's change has no movers section - it has a table. The commentary line writes itself from the shares: 'Growth this week was a Services story; the rest of the business was broadly flat.'

I want a watch-items section in the weekly pack - things that are not problems yet but are drifting toward a threshold. Our open-tickets table has an age in days and a priority. Show me how a watch item gets computed.

A watch item is a threshold with a countdown: a stock of work aging toward the point where it becomes a breach. The useful query is not the average age - averages hide tails - but the count already inside the warning band:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE open_tickets (ticket_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, age_days INTEGER NOT NULL, priority TEXT NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO open_tickets VALUES (1, 2, 'high'), (2, 5, 'normal'), (3, 9, 'normal'), (4, 12, 'high'), (5, 13, 'normal'), (6, 18, 'normal'), (7, 21, 'high'), (8, 27, 'normal'), (9, 33, 'normal'), (10, 4, 'normal'), (11, 11, 'normal'), (12, 16, 'high')
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN age_days >= 14 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS breached_14d, SUM(CASE WHEN age_days BETWEEN 10 AND 13 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS warning_band, COUNT(*) AS total_open FROM open_tickets
SELECT COUNT(*) AS high_priority_over_10d FROM open_tickets WHERE priority = 'high' AND age_days > 10

messages.content: Watch item, computed: 5 tickets are already past the 14-day line, and 3 more sit in the 10-to-13-day warning band - they breach next week unless worked, out of 12 open in total. Of the aged tickets, 3 are high priority, which is the sentence that gets the item its place on the page. This is the shape a watch item needs: a current count, a threshold, and a dated consequence ('these three breach by next pack'). Compare the average age of the queue, which would read a comfortable-looking figure pulled down by fresh tickets and would say nothing actionable. Watch items also need an exit rule: an item leaves the section when it resolves or when it breaches and moves to the problems section - a watch list that only grows becomes wallpaper, and readers learn to skip it. Review the band edges quarterly; 10 days is a judgment about how fast this team can clear aged work, not a law of nature.

The pack needs a support section: tickets opened, closed, and the backlog, for this week and last. The tickets table has opened and closed dates. Build it so the backlog figure is derived, not typed in.
Backlog is a stock, not a flow: it is last week's backlog plus opened minus closed. Deriving it in the query means the pack can never show a backlog that disagrees with the flows printed next to it:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE ticket_flow (week TEXT PRIMARY KEY, opened INTEGER NOT NULL, closed INTEGER NOT NULL, backlog_start INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO ticket_flow VALUES ('W10', 212, 198, 340), ('W11', 231, 205, 354)
SELECT week, opened, closed, backlog_start + opened - closed AS backlog_end FROM ticket_flow ORDER BY week

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
week | opened | closed | backlog_end
W10 | 212 | 198 | 354
W11 | 231 | 205 | 380

Support section: W10 closed at a backlog of 354 and W11 at 380. Opened rose from 212 to 231 while closures rose only from 198 to 205, so the queue grew by 26 tickets this week on top of last week's growth of 14. Two consecutive weeks of opened exceeding closed is the story - not the backlog level itself, which is just the accumulated consequence. Note the arithmetic discipline: the W11 row's backlog_start (354) equals W10's derived backlog_end, and the pack build should assert that equality every week. If a row ever starts at a number that does not match the prior week's derived end, tickets were reclassified, merged, or deleted outside the flow - which may be legitimate housekeeping, but it must surface as a note ('backlog restated by 12 after duplicate merge'), never as a silent discontinuity. Stocks derived from flows can be audited; stocks typed in from a dashboard cannot.
Labor cost rose this month and I need the pack bridge: how much is more hours and how much is a higher hourly rate? Hours and cost are in a monthly table.
Same bridge shape as revenue: cost is hours times rate. The hours effect values the extra hours at last month's rate; the rate effect applies the rate increase to this month's hours:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE labor_month (month TEXT PRIMARY KEY, hours REAL NOT NULL, cost_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT month, hours, cost_cents, ROUND(cost_cents / hours, 0) AS rate_cents FROM labor_month ORDER BY month

messages.content: Labor cost rose 920000 cents. The bridge: the rate went from 2300 cents an hour in February to 2400 in March. Hours effect: 575000 cents - 250 additional hours at the old rate. Rate effect: 345000 cents - the 100-cent hourly increase across all 3450 March hours. The two sum to the 920000 total. Read managerially, the hours effect is the bigger story (575000 of the 920000): the business bought more labor, which is a scheduling or demand question. The rate effect is the smaller, structural piece - it will recur every month at the new rate even if hours flatten, and the pack should say so, because next month's bridge will show a rate effect of zero and a reader comparing the two bridges might think the pay rise stopped costing money. Bridges explain changes, not levels; the level consequence of a rate rise is permanent and belongs in the commentary, not the arithmetic.

Before the pack goes out I want a freshness stamp: for each source table, the latest date it contains, so readers can see if any section is built on stale data. Our sources record their own max dates in a small registry table.
The stamp is itself a query, run at pack build time. If a source missed its load, its max date lags and the stamp shows it before a reader has to discover it from a suspiciously familiar number:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE source_freshness (source TEXT PRIMARY KEY, latest_record_date TEXT NOT NULL, expected_lag_days INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO source_freshness VALUES ('sales', '2026-03-08', 1), ('support_tickets', '2026-03-08', 1), ('inventory', '2026-03-05', 2), ('ad_spend', '2026-03-08', 1)
SELECT source, latest_record_date, CAST(julianday('2026-03-09') - julianday(latest_record_date) AS INTEGER) AS lag_days, expected_lag_days FROM source_freshness ORDER BY lag_days DESC

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
source | latest_record_date | lag_days | expected_lag_days
inventory | 2026-03-05 | 4 | 2
sales | 2026-03-08 | 1 | 1
support_tickets | 2026-03-08 | 1 | 1
ad_spend | 2026-03-08 | 1 | 1

arguments.sql: SELECT source FROM source_freshness WHERE CAST(julianday('2026-03-09') - julianday(latest_record_date) AS INTEGER) > expected_lag_days

messages.content:
Freshness stamp for the pack built March 9:
source | latest_record_date | lag_days | expected_lag_days
inventory | 2026-03-05 | 4 | 2
sales | 2026-03-08 | 1 | 1
support_tickets | 2026-03-08 | 1 | 1
ad_spend | 2026-03-08 | 1 | 1
One flag: inventory is 4 days stale against a 2-day expected lag - its feed missed at least one load. Every other source is one day behind, as designed. The pack has three honest options: delay the inventory section, publish it with the stamp visible and a 'data through March 5' note on that section, or publish and stay silent. The third is the only unacceptable one, because a reader comparing this week's inventory tile to last week's will see no change and conclude the business stood still, when in fact the data did. The stamp costs one small table and one query, and it converts a class of silent errors - the missed load - into a visible, boring annotation. Boring is the goal: freshness failures should be clerical events, not discoveries made in the exec meeting.

The pack shows revenue split into new and returning customers. This week the returning share dropped and the CEO is worried retention is slipping. I have weekly revenue by segment. Check the split before we panic.
A share can fall while the segment grows - shares are ratios, and ratios move when either side moves. The levels first, then the share:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE segment_revenue (week TEXT NOT NULL, segment TEXT NOT NULL, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO segment_revenue VALUES ('W10', 'new', 1500000), ('W10', 'returning', 3500000), ('W11', 'new', 2300000), ('W11', 'returning', 3710000)
SELECT week, SUM(CASE WHEN segment = 'returning' THEN revenue_cents END) AS returning_cents, SUM(revenue_cents) AS total_cents FROM segment_revenue GROUP BY week ORDER BY week

messages.content: Returning revenue did not fall - it grew 6%, from 3500000 to 3710000 cents. Its share fell from 70% to 61.7% because new-customer revenue grew much faster (1500000 to 2300000, a launch week doing exactly what a launch is for). The CEO's worry is a ratio illusion, and it is one of the most common pack misreadings: a falling share of a growing total gets narrated as a decline. The pack defense is presentational: wherever a share is printed, print the two levels beside it. 'Returning: 3710000 cents (61.7% of total, share down on a new-customer surge)' cannot be misread the way a bare 61.7% can. Retention questions deserve cohort data - whether January's customers came back - not segment shares, and the pack should route the CEO's real question to the cohort table rather than letting a share answer it badly.

Once a quarter I want the pack to audit itself: recompute every headline figure from the raw tables and compare against what was actually published, catching drift between the pack build and the sources. Design the audit for our revenue headline using a published-figures table and the daily sales table.

The audit treats published figures as claims and the raw tables as evidence. Any week where the recomputation differs from the published figure gets listed - the audit's output should be empty most quarters, and it earns its keep the one time it is not:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE daily_sales (day TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE published_pack (week TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO published_pack VALUES ('2026-W05', 4790000), ('2026-W06', 5780000)

SELECT p.week, p.revenue_cents AS published, SUM(d.revenue_cents) AS recomputed, SUM(d.revenue_cents) - p.revenue_cents AS difference FROM published_pack p JOIN daily_sales d ON strftime('%Y-W%W', d.day) = p.week GROUP BY p.week, p.revenue_cents HAVING difference <> 0

messages.content:
The audit found one discrepancy:
week | published | recomputed | difference
2026-W05 | 4790000 | 5790000 | 1000000
Week 2026-W05 published 4790000 cents but the daily rows recompute to 5790000 - a difference of 1000000 cents. Week W06 reconciles exactly and does not appear, which is the audit working as designed: silence means agreement. A 1000000-cent gap is not rounding; it is a week where the pack was built from a partial load or a hand-adjusted figure and never rebuilt. The audit's value is that it runs the same comparison in the quarters where nothing is wrong, so the process is trusted when it does speak. Two design points: the recomputation must be built from the raw grain (daily rows), not from the pack's own intermediate tables, or the audit only proves the pack agrees with itself; and differences get investigated to a named cause - feed gap, manual adjustment, definition change - and recorded next to the published figure, because an unexplained restatement is just a second discrepancy. Run it quarterly, publish its result in the pack itself, and let 'audited, no differences' become a line readers look for.
March revenue is down on February and the board pack draft calls it a decline. I have two years of monthly revenue. Check whether February is even the right baseline for March in this business.

The baseline is an analytical choice, and for a seasonal business the honest one is usually the same month last year. Here is March against both baselines, plus the surrounding months so the seasonal shape is visible rather than asserted:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE monthly_revenue (month TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT revenue_cents FROM monthly_revenue WHERE month = '2026-03'

messages.content: March 2026 revenue: 5210000 cents. Against February 2026 it is -4.9% - the draft's 'decline'. Against March 2025 it is 9.5% - growth. The tiebreaker is in the table: in 2025, March also fell against February (-7%), because February is this business's seasonal peak (a short month with a promotion window) and March always steps down from it. Comparing March to February measures the calendar, not the business. The pack rule: for any month with a known seasonal shape, the headline comparison is same-period-last-year, and the sequential comparison may appear only with the seasonal context attached. Neither baseline is 'the truth' in isolation - last-year comparisons can hide a genuine recent deterioration, which is why the full six-month table belongs in the appendix - but the headline must be the comparison that a change in the business, rather than a change in the month, would move.
April's revenue looks flat against March, but April had fewer business days. Can you put both months on a per-business-day footing using a daily sales table?

Totals reward months for having more selling days. The per-business-day rate removes the calendar's thumb from the scale. Business days are counted in the query - weekdays only - so the adjustment is reproducible:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE daily_sales (day TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)

SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', day) AS month, COUNT(*) AS business_days, SUM(revenue_cents) AS revenue_cents, ROUND(SUM(revenue_cents) * 1.0 / COUNT(*), 0) AS per_day_cents FROM daily_sales WHERE strftime('%w', day) BETWEEN '1' AND '5' GROUP BY month ORDER BY month

messages.content:
Per business day:
month | business_days | revenue_cents | per_day_cents
2026-03 | 10 | 4118000 | 411800
2026-04 | 8 | 3486000 | 435750
The daily rows here are all weekdays by construction of the sample, and the query's weekday filter is what enforces that on the full table. March shows 10 business days in the sample at 411800 cents per day; April shows 8 at 435750 - a per-day improvement of 5.8% that the flat monthly totals completely hid. Two cautions belong with this adjustment in the pack. First, per-day rates assume every business day is alike, which weekends-versus-weekday mixes and holiday weeks violate; a month whose business days include a public holiday is not fully adjusted by this method. Second, the adjustment answers 'are we selling more per opportunity', not 'did we make more money' - the cash still follows the totals. Report both, labeled: totals for the bank, per-day rates for the trend. A pack that shows only totals will keep congratulating long months and scolding short ones.
It is April 18 and the draft pack compares April month-to-date revenue against the whole of March, showing a scary drop. Fix the comparison properly, please.

A partial period against a full period is not a comparison; it is a countdown. The defensible versions are April-to-date against the same dates in March, and a run-rate projection that is labeled as a projection. Both, from the daily table:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE daily_sales (day TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(revenue_cents) AS apr_mtd FROM daily_sales WHERE day BETWEEN '2026-04-01' AND '2026-04-18'
SELECT SUM(revenue_cents) AS mar_same_dates FROM daily_sales WHERE day BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-18'
SELECT SUM(revenue_cents) AS mar_full FROM daily_sales WHERE strftime('%Y-%m', day) = '2026-03'

messages.content: April 1-18 revenue: 1806000 cents. Against the same 18 days of March (1719000 cents) that is +5.1% - the business is slightly ahead, not in a drop. Against the whole of March (2486000 cents) it reads as a collapse, but that comparison has 13 more selling days baked into one side of it. The run-rate projection - 1806000 scaled by 30/18 - lands at 3010000 cents for the full month, and it must be labeled a projection with its assumption showing: it assumes the remaining days sell at the same average as the first 18, which weekend mix and month-end effects routinely falsify. The pack rule for mid-period editions: compare like-for-like date ranges in the headline, put the run-rate in a clearly marked projection line, and never let a partial period stand next to a full one in the same chart without the day counts printed on both. Most 'bad month' panics in week three are this exact artifact.

Week 14 revenue spiked and week 15 slumped, and the commentary is treating it as a boom and a hangover. The spring holiday fell in week 15 this year instead of week 14. I have weekly revenue for two years - show me the holiday-shift effect.

When a holiday moves between weeks across years, it drags its revenue effect with it, and naive week comparisons read the calendar as demand. The two-year table makes the shift visible because the spike follows the holiday, not the week number:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE weekly_revenue (year INTEGER NOT NULL, week INTEGER NOT NULL, holiday_in_week INTEGER NOT NULL, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN year = 2026 THEN revenue_cents END) - SUM(CASE WHEN year = 2025 THEN revenue_cents END) AS w14_yoy FROM weekly_revenue WHERE week = 14
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN year = 2026 THEN revenue_cents END) - SUM(CASE WHEN year = 2025 THEN revenue_cents END) AS w15_yoy FROM weekly_revenue WHERE week = 15
SELECT year, SUM(revenue_cents) AS two_week_total FROM weekly_revenue WHERE week IN (14, 15) GROUP BY year ORDER BY year

messages.content: Week 14 year over year reads -320000 cents and week 15 reads +590000 - the 'hangover' and the 'boom', swapped. But combine the two weeks, which is the window that contains the holiday in both years: 2025 totals 4340000 cents and 2026 totals 4610000, growth of 6.2% with no spike and no slump anywhere. The holiday week's revenue (2410000 in 2025's week 14, 2520000 in 2026's week 15) follows the holiday, and the non-holiday weeks sit in a narrow band around 2000000 in both years. The pack fix is mechanical: for any week containing a movable holiday, the comparison unit becomes the holiday window - the two or three weeks the holiday can land in - and the commentary names the shift explicitly ('holiday fell in week 15 this year, week 14 last year'). Teams that skip this will spend one meeting a year celebrating a calendar and the next apologizing for it.
February revenue grew year over year, but a skeptic in the meeting said last February had a leap day. Monthly table has February 2024 and February 2025. Settle it with a per-day comparison.
A leap February has 29 selling days against 28 - roughly 3.6% more month. Per-day revenue is the honest comparison, and both Februaries are in the table:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE monthly_revenue (month TEXT PRIMARY KEY, days INTEGER NOT NULL, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT month, days, revenue_cents, ROUND(revenue_cents * 1.0 / days, 0) AS per_day_cents FROM monthly_revenue ORDER BY month

messages.content: The skeptic has half a point. On totals, February 2025 is -1.22% against February 2024 - a small decline. Per day, it is 2.31% ahead: 170000 cents per day in the leap February against 173929 in the 28-day one. The leap day handed 2024 an extra day of trading worth roughly a day's revenue, and comparing totals charges 2025 for a day it never had. Neither figure is a lie; they answer different questions. The pack convention worth adopting: whenever a comparison period differs in length from its baseline - leap years, 53-week years, months with different day counts - the per-day (or per-week) rate is the headline and the total is the context, with the day counts printed. It costs one extra column and it retires a whole genre of meeting argument, because the calendar stops being available as an explanation for performance in either direction.

The promo week gets compared to the same week last year, but last year's week had a competitor's store closure driving traffic to us. I have weekly revenue around the promo for both years. Give me a baseline that is not poisoned.

A baseline contaminated by a known one-off event will make a healthy promo look weak forever. The alternative baseline is the local trend: the average of the weeks surrounding the promo in the current year, compared against the same surrounding structure last year. Both baselines, side by side:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE weekly_revenue (year INTEGER NOT NULL, week INTEGER NOT NULL, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT year, revenue_cents FROM weekly_revenue WHERE week = 30 ORDER BY year
SELECT year, ROUND(AVG(revenue_cents), 0) AS surrounding_avg FROM weekly_revenue WHERE week IN (29, 31) GROUP BY year ORDER BY year

messages.content: Naive year-over-year, the promo week reads -12.3% - 2350000 against last year's 2680000 - and on that reading the promo is dying. Now the uplift reading. This year the promo week ran 15.5% above its surrounding weeks' average (2035000 cents). Last year it ran 39.2% above its surroundings (1925000) - a bigger uplift, because last year's promo week also harvested the competitor's closure traffic. So the honest statement is narrower than either headline: the promo still lifts revenue substantially, but last year's edition was flattered by a one-off event we cannot recreate, and some of its apparent decline is the baseline returning to normal. The pack rule: when a baseline period contains a known one-off, footnote it and show the alternative baseline next to the standard one. Choosing the surrounding-weeks baseline silently would be its own kind of cooking; showing both, with the reason, is analysis.
Monthly revenue dropped 8% and the commentary blames demand. There is a flag on orders for one-off project work. Split the month into recurring and one-off before we write anything.
A single project order can impersonate a demand trend in both directions - it inflates its month and then haunts the next month's comparison. The split takes one GROUP BY:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, month TEXT NOT NULL, one_off INTEGER NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)

SELECT month, SUM(CASE WHEN one_off = 0 THEN amount_cents ELSE 0 END) AS recurring_cents, SUM(CASE WHEN one_off = 1 THEN amount_cents ELSE 0 END) AS one_off_cents, SUM(amount_cents) AS total_cents FROM orders GROUP BY month ORDER BY month

messages.content:
The split:
month | recurring_cents | one_off_cents | total_cents
2026-02 | 3545000 | 655000 | 4200000
2026-03 | 3860000 | 0 | 3860000
Headline revenue did fall -8.1% - 3860000 against 4200000. But recurring revenue rose 8.9% (3545000 to 3860000). The entire decline is February's one-off project order of 655000 cents not repeating, which is not a demand signal; it is the definition of one-off. Demand, on the recurring line, is growing. Two pack disciplines follow. First, one-off items above a materiality threshold get their own line in the pack permanently, so their arrival and departure never again impersonate a trend. Second, the flag has to be applied at order entry by a rule (project-type orders, single orders above a set value), not by someone remembering in the meeting - an unflagged one-off is indistinguishable from demand until it fails to repeat. Commentary written before this split would have sent the team chasing a demand problem the business does not have.
Q1 revenue against Q4: the quarters have different numbers of days and I keep getting asked whether the growth is real. Quarterly totals and day counts are in a table - normalize it.
Ninety-two days against ninety is a 2% head start before anyone sells anything. Per-day revenue strips that out:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE quarterly_revenue (quarter TEXT PRIMARY KEY, days INTEGER NOT NULL, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO quarterly_revenue VALUES ('2025-Q4', 92, 14950000), ('2026-Q1', 90, 14850000)
SELECT quarter, days, revenue_cents, ROUND(revenue_cents * 1.0 / days, 0) AS per_day_cents FROM quarterly_revenue ORDER BY quarter

messages.content: On totals, Q1 is -0.67% against Q4 - flat to slightly down. Per day, Q1 is 1.54% ahead: 162500 cents a day across Q4's 92 days against 165000 across Q1's 90. The quarter grew; the calendar shrank faster. This is the same leap-day lesson at quarter scale, and it recurs constantly - Q1 is structurally the shortest quarter and will lose most total comparisons against Q4 regardless of performance. The pack convention: quarter comparisons carry the day counts in the column headers ('Q1, 90 days') and the per-day rate as the headline trend figure. Cash planning still uses totals, because rent is not charged per day of revenue - the two figures serve two different questions, and labeling which question each answers is most of what a good pack does.
March year over year: revenue is up 12%. I want to know if that is price or volume before the board meeting. Orders, revenue, and a units figure for both Marches are in the table.

The bridge again, this time across years: orders effect at last year's order value, and rate effect on this year's orders. If most of the 12% is rate, the growth has a different shelf life than if it is volume:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE march_comparison (year INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, orders INTEGER NOT NULL, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO march_comparison VALUES (2025, 4200, 29400000), (2026, 4500, 32940000)
SELECT year, orders, revenue_cents, ROUND(revenue_cents * 1.0 / orders, 0) AS aov_cents FROM march_comparison ORDER BY year

messages.content: March revenue rose 3540000 cents year over year. Average order value went from 7000 cents to 7320. Volume effect: 2100000 cents - 300 more orders at last year's AOV. Rate effect: 1440000 cents - the 320-cent AOV increase across this year's 4500 orders. The effects sum to the full change. So the 12% is roughly 59% volume and 41% rate: the business sold more orders and got more per order, in that order of importance. For the board, that ordering is the message - volume-led growth suggests the demand is there; a year where the bridge runs 90% rate is a year of charging the same customers more, which works until it doesn't. Run this bridge on every year-over-year headline in the pack, not only revenue: cost lines decompose the same way (units times unit cost), and a cost increase that is mostly volume is a success story wearing a worrying costume.

I am writing the comparisons footnote for the pack and I want it to be evidence-based: which baseline does each of our headline KPIs use, and why? Pull the current registry rows for the reporting KPIs so the footnote quotes them rather than my memory.
The footnote should be generated from the same registry the dashboard is held to - then it cannot drift from the definitions in force. Here are the reporting KPIs' registered comparison baselines:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE kpi_definitions (kpi TEXT NOT NULL, version INTEGER NOT NULL, baseline TEXT NOT NULL, baseline_reason TEXT NOT NULL, effective_from TEXT NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO kpi_definitions VALUES ('revenue', 3, 'same period last year', 'strong seasonal shape', '2025-01-01'), ('orders', 2, 'same period last year', 'strong seasonal shape', '2025-01-01'), ('backlog', 1, 'prior week', 'stock measure, trend is weekly', '2025-01-01'), ('sla_attainment', 2, 'prior month', 'low seasonality, staffing-driven', '2025-06-01'), ('inventory_days', 1, 'prior month', 'managed level, not seasonal', '2025-01-01')
SELECT kpi, version, baseline, baseline_reason FROM kpi_definitions ORDER BY kpi

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
kpi | version | baseline | baseline_reason
backlog | 1 | prior week | stock measure, trend is weekly
inventory_days | 1 | prior month | managed level, not seasonal
orders | 2 | same period last year | strong seasonal shape
revenue | 3 | same period last year | strong seasonal shape
sla_attainment | 2 | prior month | low seasonality, staffing-driven

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS seasonal_baseline_kpis FROM kpi_definitions WHERE baseline = 'same period last year'

messages.content:
The registry's comparison baselines:
kpi | version | baseline | baseline_reason
backlog | 1 | prior week | stock measure, trend is weekly
inventory_days | 1 | prior month | managed level, not seasonal
orders | 2 | same period last year | strong seasonal shape
revenue | 3 | same period last year | strong seasonal shape
sla_attainment | 2 | prior month | low seasonality, staffing-driven
2 of the 5 reporting KPIs - revenue and orders - use same-period-last-year, because their registered reason is a strong seasonal shape. The other three use short baselines deliberately: backlog is a stock whose story is its weekly direction, SLA attainment is staffing-driven with low seasonality, and inventory days is a managed level. That mix is the footnote's real content: the baseline is chosen per KPI from how the quantity behaves, not applied uniformly for tidiness. A pack that compares everything to last month will manufacture seasonal alarms; a pack that compares everything to last year will sleep through a sudden deterioration in a stock measure. Generating the footnote from the registry also means that when a baseline changes - say SLA attainment develops seasonality as the product grows - the change is a versioned registry row and the footnote updates itself, instead of relying on someone remembering to edit prose.
Our dashboard's channel tiles add up to more than the revenue tile. Orders have channel flags and some orders seem to be counted twice. I have the orders table - find the overlap.

When tiles sum past the total, the usual cause is a grain problem: an order that belongs to two channels gets counted by both tiles, while the revenue tile counts it once. The orders table carries one flag per channel, so the overlap is directly countable:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, via_web INTEGER NOT NULL, via_phone INTEGER NOT NULL, via_store INTEGER NOT NULL)

SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS ledger_total, SUM(CASE WHEN via_web = 1 THEN amount_cents ELSE 0 END) AS web_tile, SUM(CASE WHEN via_phone = 1 THEN amount_cents ELSE 0 END) AS phone_tile, SUM(CASE WHEN via_store = 1 THEN amount_cents ELSE 0 END) AS store_tile FROM orders
SELECT COUNT(*) AS dual_channel_orders, SUM(amount_cents) AS overlap_cents FROM orders WHERE via_web + via_phone + via_store > 1

messages.content: Found it. The ledger total is 563000 cents. The channel tiles read web 359000, phone 250000, store 93000 - summing to 702000, which is 139000 cents more than the ledger. That excess is exactly the 2 dual-channel orders (orders 4 and 8, started on the web and completed by phone), counted once by each of their two tiles. Neither tile is wrong about its own channel; the dashboard is wrong to present channel tiles as a partition of revenue when the channels overlap. Three honest fixes: assign each order a single primary channel by a stated rule (completing channel wins, say) so the tiles partition; or relabel the tiles as 'orders touched by' measures that are explicitly non-additive; or add an 'of which multi-channel' line. What not to do is quietly force the tiles to sum by netting the overlap out of one channel - that hides real customer behavior (web research, phone close is a pattern worth seeing) inside an arithmetic patch.
A tile on our dashboard has shown the same inventory figure for days. There is a refresh log table with one row per tile per refresh. Audit the tiles' freshness for me.
A dashboard rarely announces that it is stale; the numbers just stop moving. The refresh log makes staleness a query instead of a suspicion:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE tile_refresh_log (tile TEXT NOT NULL, refreshed_at TEXT NOT NULL)
SELECT tile, MAX(refreshed_at) AS last_refresh FROM tile_refresh_log GROUP BY tile ORDER BY last_refresh
SELECT tile, CAST(julianday('2026-03-09 12:00') - julianday(MAX(refreshed_at)) AS INTEGER) AS days_stale FROM tile_refresh_log GROUP BY tile ORDER BY days_stale DESC LIMIT 1

messages.content:
Last refresh per tile:
tile | last_refresh
inventory_days | 2026-03-06 06:00
orders | 2026-03-09 12:00
revenue | 2026-03-09 12:00
sla | 2026-03-09 12:00
The inventory_days tile is 3 days stale - it last refreshed on March 6 while the rest of the board is current to midday March 9. Its unchanging figure was not stability; it was a dead feed, and anyone who made a stocking decision from it this week was reading last week's shelves. Two design fixes. First, every tile should carry its own as-of timestamp in its corner, rendered from this log, so staleness is visible at the point of reading rather than discoverable by audit. Second, the refresh job should alert on absence, not just on failure: this feed did not error, it simply stopped being scheduled, and a monitor that only watches for error codes will never notice silence. A dashboard's trustworthiness is mostly this unglamorous layer - a board where every number is fresh except one is more dangerous than a board that is entirely down, because the down board at least admits it.

The dashboard's headline revenue tile does not equal the sum of the regional tiles, and everyone swears the same region filter is applied everywhere. I have a tile definitions table and the sales data. Prove where the filter is not applying.
Swearing is not a check. The definitions table records each tile's filter as data, and the sales table can be summed under each tile's actual filter - the mismatch will localize itself:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE tile_definitions (tile TEXT PRIMARY KEY, region_filter TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE sales (sale_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, region TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO tile_definitions VALUES ('headline_revenue', 'ALL'), ('north_tile', 'North'), ('south_tile', 'South'), ('east_tile', 'East'), ('west_tile', 'West')
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS headline_all, SUM(CASE WHEN region IN ('North', 'South', 'East', 'West') THEN amount_cents ELSE 0 END) AS four_regions FROM sales
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS unassigned_cents FROM sales WHERE region = 'Online-Unassigned'

messages.content: The headline tile, filtered to ALL regions, reads 1093000 cents. The four regional tiles sum to 959000. The difference is exactly 134000 cents: sales whose region is 'Online-Unassigned', a value the regional tiles' filters do not cover. Nobody misapplied a filter - the filter set itself has a hole, because the business grew a channel that the region taxonomy never absorbed. This is the most common shape of dashboard inconsistency: not a bug in any tile, but a category that exists in the data and not in the reporting model. The fixes are governance, not arithmetic: either assign online sales a region by rule (customer's region, fulfillment region - a business decision, stated in the definition), or give the dashboard a fifth tile so the total visibly partitions. And add the standing check this incident teaches: sum of parts versus headline, run at every build, with any residual required to be a named category. An unexplained residual is a hole in the taxonomy, and it will grow.

Clicking into the revenue tile shows detail rows that do not add up to the tile. The tile query and the drill query were written by different people. Orders table has a category column with some NULLs. Reconcile them.

A drill-down that does not reconcile teaches users to distrust the tile - or worse, to trust the drill. The classic cause is a filter present in one query and not the other, and NULL categories are the classic hiding place:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, category TEXT, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'Hardware', 45000), (2, 'Services', 62000), (3, 'Hardware', 38000), (4, NULL, 21000), (5, 'Digital', 54000), (6, 'Services', 47000), (7, NULL, 16000), (8, 'Digital', 33000), (9, 'Hardware', 51000), (10, 'Services', 29000)
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS tile_total FROM orders
SELECT category, SUM(amount_cents) AS cat_total FROM orders WHERE category IS NOT NULL GROUP BY category ORDER BY category
SELECT COUNT(*) AS uncategorized_orders, SUM(amount_cents) AS uncategorized_cents FROM orders WHERE category IS NULL

messages.content:
The tile reads 396000 cents. The drill rows:
category | cat_total
Digital | 87000
Hardware | 134000
Services | 138000
They sum to 359000 - short of the tile by exactly 37000 cents, the value of the 2 orders whose category is NULL. The drill query filters NULL categories out (deliberately or by accident of a WHERE clause), while the tile counts everything. Both queries are internally correct; the pair is incoherent, and incoherence between a number and its own explanation is the fastest way to lose a dashboard's audience. The fix has two parts. Technically: the drill gains an explicit 'Uncategorized' bucket so the parts always sum to the tile - hiding the bucket does not reduce the uncategorized orders, it just hides them. Operationally: 2 uncategorized orders out of 10 is a data-entry problem worth its own line in the pack until it shrinks. And adopt the standing rule this teaches: every drill-down ships with a reconciliation assertion - parts sum to tile, run at build time - so the next divergence is caught by the build, not by a skeptical reader in a meeting.

I want to hold the dashboard to the definition registry: every tile must trace to a registered KPI definition, and I want a report of tiles that cannot. There is a tiles table and the registry. Run the contract check.

The check is an anti-join: tiles whose KPI name has no registry row are numbers without a contract. Tiles whose registered version differs from the version the tile claims are the subtler failure, so the check reports both:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE dashboard_tiles (tile TEXT PRIMARY KEY, kpi TEXT NOT NULL, claimed_version INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE kpi_definitions (kpi TEXT NOT NULL, version INTEGER NOT NULL, effective_from TEXT NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO dashboard_tiles VALUES ('Revenue', 'revenue', 3), ('Orders', 'orders', 2), ('Refund rate', 'refund_rate', 1), ('Engagement score', 'engagement_score', 1), ('Backlog', 'backlog', 1), ('SLA attainment', 'sla_attainment', 2)

INSERT INTO kpi_definitions VALUES ('revenue', 3, '2025-01-01'), ('orders', 2, '2025-01-01'), ('refund_rate', 1, '2025-07-01'), ('refund_rate', 2, '2026-01-01'), ('backlog', 1, '2025-01-01'), ('sla_attainment', 2, '2025-06-01')
SELECT t.tile, t.kpi FROM dashboard_tiles t LEFT JOIN kpi_definitions d ON d.kpi = t.kpi WHERE d.kpi IS NULL

SELECT t.tile, t.claimed_version, MAX(d.version) AS current_version FROM dashboard_tiles t JOIN kpi_definitions d ON d.kpi = t.kpi GROUP BY t.tile, t.claimed_version HAVING t.claimed_version <> MAX(d.version)

messages.content: Contract check results. Orphan tile: Engagement score, built on the KPI 'engagement_score', which has no registry row at all - nobody can say what it counts, and it should come off the board until someone writes its definition down. Stale-version tile: Refund rate claims definition version 1 but the registry's current version is 2 - the tile was never rebuilt when refund rate's definition changed in January, so it has been reporting the old KPI under the new name for a full quarter. That second failure is the dangerous one: the number moved in January and the commentary invented business explanations for what was actually a definition change nobody applied. The other four tiles trace cleanly. Run this check at every dashboard build and print its result in the pack's appendix. A dashboard is a set of promises about what its numbers mean; the registry is where the promises are written, and this check is how you know the board is keeping them.

Two tiles disagree about order count: the sales tile says 128 orders and the fulfillment tile says 341. One counts orders and the other counts order lines, I suspect. The data has an orders table and a lines table - confirm the grain mismatch.
Grain mismatches are the quietest dashboard bug: both tiles are right about different things and both are labeled 'orders'. The counts at each grain, from the same data:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, placed_date TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE order_lines (line_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_id INTEGER NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)

SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders) AS orders_grain, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM order_lines) AS lines_grain, (SELECT ROUND(COUNT(*) * 1.0 / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders), 2) FROM order_lines) AS lines_per_order

messages.content: Confirmed. In this sample the orders grain counts 6 and the lines grain counts 13 - 2.17 lines per order. On your board the same mismatch at full scale is what puts 128 and 341 side by side; neither tile is broken, but the fulfillment tile's label is. Grain errors survive because each tile looks plausible in isolation - the numbers only contradict when placed side by side, which is what dashboards do. The fixes are labeling and definition: the fulfillment tile becomes 'order lines picked', the sales tile stays 'orders', and both KPIs get registry rows that state their grain in the first line of the definition ('one row per order' / 'one row per order line'). Any rate built across grains - revenue per order computed from line-grain revenue over order-grain counts is fine, but a count divided by a count of a different grain is not - should be treated as a defect on sight. When two tiles disagree, ask for their grains before asking for their queries.

INSERT INTO category_revenue VALUES ('Hardware', 150050), ('Services', 220050), ('Digital', 98050), ('Consumables', 76025)
SELECT category, ROUND(amount_cents / 100.0) AS dollars FROM category_revenue ORDER BY category

category | dollars
Consumables | 760
Digital | 981
Hardware | 1501
Services | 2201

The categories in rounded dollars:

Consumables | 760
