The failure mode to avoid is an analyst 'fixing' the dollar by adjusting a category, which converts an honest rounding artifact into a falsified figure. If a reader's spreadsheet sums the displayed dollars and finds the gap, the footnote is the whole answer, and it should have been there before they asked.

Our two revenue tiles disagree every morning and agree by midday. One groups orders by UTC date and the other by local date. Orders have UTC timestamps and our local offset is minus 5 hours. Show me the orders that flip days.

A day boundary is a definition, and two tiles using different boundaries will disagree about exactly the orders near midnight - then agree once nobody is looking at the seam. The flippers are the orders whose local date differs from their UTC date:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, placed_utc TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT order_id, placed_utc, date(placed_utc) AS utc_day, date(placed_utc, '-5 hours') AS local_day FROM orders WHERE date(placed_utc) <> date(placed_utc, '-5 hours')

SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN date(placed_utc) = '2026-03-08' THEN amount_cents ELSE 0 END) AS utc_mar8, SUM(CASE WHEN date(placed_utc, '-5 hours') = '2026-03-08' THEN amount_cents ELSE 0 END) AS local_mar8 FROM orders

messages.content:
The orders that change days under the local boundary:
order_id | placed_utc | utc_day | local_day
1 | 2026-03-08 02:30 | 2026-03-08 | 2026-03-07
4 | 2026-03-09 01:10 | 2026-03-09 | 2026-03-08
5 | 2026-03-09 04:45 | 2026-03-09 | 2026-03-08
Three orders placed in the first five hours of the UTC day belong to the previous local day. So March 8 reads 145000 cents on the UTC tile and 218000 on the local tile - a 73000-cent disagreement manufactured entirely by the boundary. By midday the argument moves on because both tiles are 'about' the same business, but the seam never closes; it just migrates to the next midnight. The business has to pick one day boundary for reporting - local business date is the usual choice for an operation that opens and closes - and register it in the KPI definitions, because 'revenue by day' is meaningless until the day is defined. Source systems may keep UTC (they should), but the reporting layer converts once, in one place, and every tile inherits the conversion. Two tiles converting independently will eventually use different offsets, different DST handling, or different boundaries, and the morning argument becomes permanent.

Revenue on the dashboard jumped 30% the day we added a shipments join to the tile query, and nobody believes it. Orders and shipments tables are here - one order can have several shipments. Show the fan-out.
Joining a one-to-many table multiplies the one side's rows. If the measure being summed lives on the one side, the join inflates it by the number of matches. The reproduction is exact:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE shipments (shipment_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_id INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS true_revenue FROM orders
SELECT SUM(o.amount_cents) AS joined_revenue, COUNT(*) AS joined_rows FROM orders o JOIN shipments s ON s.order_id = o.order_id

messages.content: True revenue: 237000 cents across 4 orders. The joined query returns 401000 cents across 7 rows - order 2 counted twice (two shipments) and order 4 counted three times, adding a phantom 164000 cents. On a bigger table with a typical shipment distribution, that is your 30%. The diagnostic signature of fan-out is that the joined row count exceeds the base table's row count while the query's author believes they are still counting orders; the check - compare COUNT(*) before and after any join added to a reporting query - takes seconds and belongs in the review checklist for every tile change. The correct patterns: aggregate shipments to one row per order before joining, or sum the order amount over a DISTINCT order set, or move the measure to the shipment grain and accept that the tile now reports per-shipment economics. What never works is leaving the join in and dividing by an average fan-out factor - the factor varies by order, and the correction manufactures smaller errors everywhere to hide one big one.

Design the dashboard's build-time integrity suite as queries: one pass over our current board data that reports, per check, pass or fail with the offending figure. Use the tables we have discussed: orders with NULL categories, a tile refresh log, and a published headline to compare against.

The suite runs four checks at build time: drill reconciliation (parts sum to tile), categorization completeness, freshness, and headline agreement with the raw grain. Each check returns its own verdict row so the build can fail loudly on any one of them:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, category TEXT, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE tile_refresh_log (tile TEXT NOT NULL, refreshed_at TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE published_headline (figure TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'Hardware', 45000), (2, 'Services', 62000), (3, 'Hardware', 38000), (4, NULL, 21000), (5, 'Digital', 54000), (6, 'Services', 47000)
INSERT INTO tile_refresh_log VALUES ('revenue', '2026-03-09 06:00'), ('inventory_days', '2026-03-04 06:00')
INSERT INTO published_headline VALUES ('revenue', 246000)
SELECT CASE WHEN (SELECT SUM(amount_cents) FROM orders WHERE category IS NOT NULL) = (SELECT SUM(amount_cents) FROM orders) THEN 'pass' ELSE 'fail' END AS drill_reconciliation
SELECT CASE WHEN (SELECT value_cents FROM published_headline WHERE figure = 'revenue') = (SELECT SUM(amount_cents) FROM orders) THEN 'pass' ELSE 'fail' END AS headline_agreement
SELECT tile, CASE WHEN CAST(julianday('2026-03-09') - julianday(MAX(refreshed_at)) AS INTEGER) <= 1 THEN 'pass' ELSE 'fail' END AS freshness FROM tile_refresh_log GROUP BY tile ORDER BY tile

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
tile | freshness
inventory_days | fail
revenue | pass

Suite results on today's data: drill reconciliation - fail; headline agreement - fail; freshness - inventory_days fail, revenue pass. Three failures, all previously seen in this board's history: the drill does not reconcile because a NULL-category order is filtered out of the parts; the headline disagrees with the raw orders sum by the same order's value, which tells you the headline and the drill were built from the same filtered query (one root cause surfacing in two checks is a clue, not a coincidence); and the inventory tile is five days stale. The suite's design principles: checks compare independent paths to the same figure (tile versus raw grain, parts versus whole), each check names the offending value rather than just failing, and the build publishes the suite's results alongside the board. A board that displays its own integrity status earns the right to be believed on the days everything passes - and gets fixed faster on the days it does not.

The pack needs a proper cohort table: signups grouped by their signup week, with how many were still active one and two weeks later. Our users table has activity flags per user. Build the cohort view.

A cohort table groups people by when they started and follows that fixed group forward - the membership never changes, which is what makes it honest. Here it is built from per-user flags for activity in the first and second weeks after signup:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE users (user_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, cohort_week TEXT NOT NULL, active_week1 INTEGER NOT NULL, active_week2 INTEGER NOT NULL)

SELECT cohort_week, COUNT(*) AS cohort_size, SUM(active_week1) AS active_w1, SUM(active_week2) AS active_w2, ROUND(SUM(active_week2) * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 1) AS retained_w2_pct FROM users GROUP BY cohort_week ORDER BY cohort_week

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
cohort_week | cohort_size | active_w1 | active_w2 | retained_w2_pct
W05 | 5 | 4 | 2 | 40
W06 | 6 | 5 | 3 | 50
W07 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 50

The cohort table:
cohort_week | cohort_size | active_w1 | active_w2 | retained_w2_pct
W05 | 5 | 4 | 2 | 40
W06 | 6 | 5 | 3 | 50
W07 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 50
Read it by rows for a cohort's life and by columns for a stage's trend. The week-2 retention column is the pack's story: W05 retained 40% of its cohort into week 2, W06 50%, W07 50% - the newest cohort is holding better at the same age, which is the only fair way to compare cohorts (same age, not same calendar date). Two disciplines keep this table honest. The diagonal problem: W07's week-2 figure could only be measured once those users had lived two weeks, so in the pack this table is published on a lag and the freshest cohort's later columns are marked not-yet-measurable rather than filled with partial counts. And the cohort size column matters: W07's improvement rests on 4 users, so the pack should show sizes beside every rate - a percentage on a tiny cohort is a rumor with a decimal point.
Our funnel has four stages - visit, signup, trial, paid - and I track stage counts by week. Overall conversion looks flat but I suspect one stage is leaking more over time. Find it.
Overall conversion can sit still while stages trade places underneath it. The stage-to-stage rates by week are the diagnostic; the leak is the stage whose rate trends down:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE funnel_weekly (week TEXT NOT NULL, stage TEXT NOT NULL, users INTEGER NOT NULL)

SELECT week, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN stage = 'trial' THEN users END) / SUM(CASE WHEN stage = 'signup' THEN users END), 1) AS signup_to_trial_pct, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN stage = 'paid' THEN users END) / SUM(CASE WHEN stage = 'trial' THEN users END), 1) AS trial_to_paid_pct FROM funnel_weekly GROUP BY week ORDER BY week

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
week | signup_to_trial_pct | trial_to_paid_pct
W08 | 60 | 40
W09 | 55.9 | 41.5
W10 | 52.1 | 43.3

Overall visit-to-paid conversion barely moved: 3.6% in W08 to 3.31% in W10. The stage rates tell the real story:
week | signup_to_trial_pct | trial_to_paid_pct
W08 | 60 | 40
W09 | 55.9 | 41.5
W10 | 52.1 | 43.3
Signup-to-trial fell from 60% to 52.1% across the three weeks - a steady leak - while trial-to-paid actually improved from 40% to 43.3%, masking the leak in the overall figure. More visits and a better closing stage are compensating for a worsening middle. This is why the pack tracks stage rates, not just the end-to-end number: the end-to-end figure is a product of the stages, and products hide offsetting movements. The investigation now has an address - whatever changed in the signup-to-trial step over these weeks (an email delay, a form change, a slower provisioning step) - and the pack's funnel section should carry the stage rates with the leaking stage flagged by trend, not by someone remembering to look. A funnel reported only at its ends is a story with the middle torn out.
Confusing month: our period activation rate improved, but the retention team says the February cohort is the worst in months. Both use the same users data. Show me how both can be true.

They can both be true because they measure different things. The period rate counts everyone who activated in February, whenever they signed up. The cohort rate follows February's signups specifically. When the mix of who is activating shifts, the two part company:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE cohort_quality (cohort_month TEXT PRIMARY KEY, signups INTEGER NOT NULL, activated_within_7d INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE period_activity (month TEXT PRIMARY KEY, signups INTEGER NOT NULL, activations INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO cohort_quality VALUES ('2026-01', 1000, 420), ('2026-02', 1400, 476)
INSERT INTO period_activity VALUES ('2026-01', 1000, 405), ('2026-02', 1400, 574)

messages.content: Cohort view: January's signups activated at 42%; February's at 34% - the retention team is right, February's cohort is markedly weaker. Period view: activations per signup in the month rose from 40.5% to 41% - the period reporter is also right. The reconciliation is in what the period numerator contains: February's 574 activations include January signups who activated late, during February, while February's own large signup wave (1400, up 40% on a campaign) activated poorly. The period metric improved because the denominator and numerator describe different populations; the cohort metric deteriorated because February's campaign bought lower-intent signups. This is the cohort-versus-period distinction the pack must respect: period metrics answer 'what happened this month', cohort metrics answer 'how good is what we acquired this month', and confusing the two lets a growth campaign borrow credit from last month's quality while hiding its own. When the two disagree, believe the cohort table about acquisition quality and the period table about operational load - and print both, labeled.

For the pack I want cohort revenue: for each signup month, average revenue per user in their first, second, and third months. The data is a cohort summary table with cohort sizes and monthly revenue totals in cents.
Cohort revenue curves show whether newer customers are worth more or less than older ones at the same age - the comparison that tells you if acquisition quality is compounding or diluting:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE cohort_revenue (cohort_month TEXT PRIMARY KEY, users INTEGER NOT NULL, month1_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, month2_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, month3_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)

SELECT cohort_month, ROUND(month1_cents * 1.0 / users, 0) AS m1_per_user, ROUND(month2_cents * 1.0 / users, 0) AS m2_per_user, ROUND(month3_cents * 1.0 / users, 0) AS m3_per_user FROM cohort_revenue ORDER BY cohort_month

messages.content:
Revenue per user by cohort age:
cohort_month | m1_per_user | m2_per_user | m3_per_user
2025-11 | 1200 | 1100 | 1050
2025-12 | 1200 | 1100 | 1050
2026-01 | 1150 | 1020 | 950
Two patterns. Within every cohort, per-user revenue decays with age - November goes 1200 to 1100 to 1050 cents - the normal shape of churn and downgrade. Across cohorts at the same age, the newest cohort starts lower: January's month-1 figure of 1150 cents is -4.2% against November's 1200. January's users are individually worth less from day one, even though January's total cohort revenue is higher because the cohort is bigger (900 users against 800). That is the dilution pattern the pack exists to catch early: growth celebrated on totals while unit value quietly slides, usually because acquisition widened into a cheaper segment. The cohort curve is the antidote because it compares like ages. One discipline: month-3 figures for the January cohort were only complete in April, so this table publishes on a lag like every cohort view - a curve with its newest points estimated is worse than a curve that is honestly two months behind.

Our funnel report shows more people at the 'paid' stage than at 'trial' for one source, which should be impossible if everyone passes through trial. Events table has stage events by source. Explain what the funnel is actually counting.

A funnel built from stage events counts events, not people passing a gate - and if some users reach paid without a trial event (direct purchase, migrated accounts, a tracking gap), the stages stop being nested and the funnel shape breaks. The counts by source expose it:

SELECT source, SUM(CASE WHEN stage = 'trial' THEN events END) AS trial_events, SUM(CASE WHEN stage = 'paid' THEN events END) AS paid_events FROM stage_events GROUP BY source ORDER BY source

source | trial_events | paid_events
ads | 640 | 288
organic | 900 | 410

By source:
source | trial_events | paid_events

The partner channel onboards customers through a reseller flow that skips the trial product entirely, so those customers legitimately never fire a trial event. The reporting fixes: either give the partner flow its own funnel (its stages are quote, contract, paid), or define the combined funnel's stages as states every customer passes through (registered, activated, paying) rather than product-specific steps. What the pack must stop doing is computing a partner 'trial-to-paid conversion' - a ratio of two numbers from different populations, which will read over 100% and teach readers to ignore the funnel entirely. Funnels are per-path instruments. When a new path appears, the honest response is a second funnel, not a wider first one.

Trial conversion by cohort: for each month's trial starts, the share that converted to paid within 30 days. Trials table has start month and a converted-within-30 flag. Build it for the pack, with cohort sizes visible.

The funnel's signup-to-trial stage dropped sharply this week. Before we blame the product, drill the stage by device - events are in a table with stage, device, and week. Localize the leak.
A stage drop concentrated in one segment is usually an instrumentation or compatibility event; a drop spread evenly is usually a product or demand event. The drill distinguishes them in one query:

Signups tripled on Tuesday according to the pack draft. Before anyone celebrates, I need the spike investigated: signups table has source and day. Separate a real event from a data fault.

A spike has two families of explanation - the world did something, or the pipeline did. The drill that separates them is concentration: real events are usually broad or traceable to one real source; faults are usually one source, one pattern, one suspicious shape:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE signups (signup_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, day TEXT NOT NULL, source TEXT NOT NULL)
SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS signups FROM signups GROUP BY day ORDER BY day
SELECT source, COUNT(*) AS signups FROM signups WHERE day = '2026-03-03' GROUP BY source ORDER BY signups DESC

messages.content:
Signups by day:
day | signups
2026-03-02 | 3
2026-03-03 | 9
2026-03-04 | 3
Tuesday's spike is entirely one source: partner contributed 7 of Tuesday's 9 signups, against 0 on Monday and 1 on Wednesday. A genuine partner launch could do this - but so could a partner feed replaying a batch or sending duplicates, and the two demand opposite responses (celebrate versus delete and restate). The next checks, in order: do the Tuesday partner signups have distinct emails and timestamps spread across the day, or identical payloads clustered in one minute? Did the partner confirm a campaign? Did those signups activate at normal rates a week later - the verdict that settles it retrospectively? Until the first two are answered, the pack prints the spike with a flag: 'Tuesday signups elevated by a single-source surge, under verification.' A pack that celebrates unverified spikes teaches the organization to manufacture them; a pack that flags them teaches sources to send clean data. The drill took one GROUP BY - concentration analysis is the cheapest fraud and fault detector in reporting.

Thursday's sales in the pack are zero and the weekly average quietly absorbed it. The daily table shows Thursday missing entirely rather than zero. Show me how the pack should treat a missing feed day.

A missing row and a zero row are different facts with different meanings, and averaging over a missing day understates every rate in the pack. First, prove the day is missing rather than zero, using a calendar spine:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE daily_sales (day TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE calendar_days (day TEXT PRIMARY KEY)
SELECT c.day AS missing_day FROM calendar_days c LEFT JOIN daily_sales d ON d.day = c.day WHERE d.day IS NULL
SELECT ROUND(AVG(revenue_cents), 0) AS avg_over_present_days FROM daily_sales

messages.content: The gap check finds 2026-03-05 missing from the sales table - Thursday March 5 has no row at all. That is a feed failure, not a zero-sales day: a real zero would be a row with 0, and a business that traded would leave one. The average over present days is 412667 cents; had the build silently treated the missing day as zero, the 'weekly average' would have read 353714 - a figure describing neither trading nor the feed. Pack rules for missing days, in order: the build checks every expected day against a calendar spine (this LEFT JOIN) and fails loudly on a gap; the pack either waits for the feed or publishes with the day explicitly marked 'no data' and all averages computed over present days and labeled as such; and the gap is logged against the source's reliability record, because a feed that drops a day a quarter is a different vendor conversation than one that drops a day a week. Zero is a measurement. Missing is an incident. A pack that cannot tell them apart will eventually report a catastrophe as a bad day and a bad day as a catastrophe.

Finance restated February: late corrections added revenue that arrived after we published. The pack printed 4,850,000 cents for February and the corrected figure is higher. I have a corrections table. Work out the restatement and how the pack should present it.

Restatements are normal in any system with late-arriving data; hiding them is what corrodes trust. The pack's job is to publish the corrected figure, mark the change, and keep the originally published figure on record:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE published_figures (month TEXT PRIMARY KEY, published_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE corrections (correction_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, month TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, reason TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO published_figures VALUES ('2026-02', 4850000)
INSERT INTO corrections VALUES (1, '2026-02', 62000, 'late settlement file'), (2, '2026-02', 18500, 'misclassified refund reversed'), (3, '2026-02', -12000, 'duplicate order removed')

SELECT p.month, p.published_cents, p.published_cents + SUM(c.amount_cents) AS restated_cents, SUM(c.amount_cents) AS net_correction FROM published_figures p JOIN corrections c ON c.month = p.month GROUP BY p.month, p.published_cents

messages.content: February restated: published 4850000 cents, net correction +68500, restated figure 4918500 cents - a 1.41% revision. The corrections are itemized: two additions (a late settlement file and a reversed misclassification) and one removal (a duplicate order), and the net is small because they partly offset - which is exactly why the pack shows the items, not just the net: a net of +68500 built from +80500 and -12000 is a healthier system than one built from a single +68500 plug. Presentation rules: the current pack prints the restated figure with a restatement note naming the month, the size, and the causes in one line each; the originally published figure stays in the published-figures table forever, never overwritten, so any old commentary remains interpretable; and a running restatement rate (this is the third restated month this year, say) is itself a data-quality metric worth a pack line. Readers forgive corrections. They do not forgive discovering that history was silently edited.

Our anomaly alerts fire so often that the team ignores them. The alert history table has the metric's weekly values and which weeks alerted at the current threshold of a 15% move. Audit the alert history and propose a threshold from the data's own variance.

An alert that fires a third of the time is not an alert; it is a subscription. The audit counts the firing rate and looks at the distribution of normal moves, so the new threshold can be set where ordinary weeks rarely cross it:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE alert_history (week TEXT PRIMARY KEY, wow_change_pct REAL NOT NULL, alerted INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS weeks, SUM(alerted) AS alerts, ROUND(AVG(ABS(wow_change_pct)), 1) AS mean_abs_move, MAX(ABS(wow_change_pct)) AS max_abs_move FROM alert_history
SELECT COUNT(*) AS would_alert_at_25 FROM alert_history WHERE ABS(wow_change_pct) >= 25

messages.content: Alert audit: 4 alerts in 12 weeks - a 33% firing rate. The mean absolute weekly move is 8.9%, and the largest move in the quarter is 18.9%. A 15% threshold on a metric that routinely swings 5-9% and touched 18.9% in a normal quarter is calibrated to cry wolf: the four alerts it produced were all, on investigation, ordinary volatility, which is why the team scrolls past them now. At a 25% threshold the same history produces 0 alerts - arguably too quiet, since a genuine 19% break would pass silently. The principled setting is between: roughly two to two and a half times the mean absolute move - here, around 18-22% - reviewed quarterly against the firing rate, with a target of alerting in perhaps one week in ten. Two more disciplines: every alert gets a recorded disposition (real event, data fault, ordinary volatility) so the threshold can be tuned on outcomes rather than vibes, and a second, tighter alert on the metric's level (not just its change) catches slow drifts that week-over-week thresholds never see. An alerting system is a reporting product too, and its KPI is the share of alerts that mattered.
A number in this week's pack looks wrong to me - orders are up but revenue per order fell off a cliff. Orders summary by week is in a table. Sanity-check it before the pack ships.

The pre-ship sanity check is a small set of ratio and bounds tests: derived figures should move within plausible ranges, and a ratio that leaves its historical band is a build error until proven otherwise:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE weekly_orders (week TEXT PRIMARY KEY, orders INTEGER NOT NULL, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT week, ROUND(revenue_cents * 1.0 / orders, 0) AS aov_cents FROM weekly_orders ORDER BY week

messages.content:
Average order value by week:
week | aov_cents
W08 | 7000
W09 | 7000
W10 | 7065
W11 | 4696
W08 through W10 sit in a tight band around 7000 cents. W11 prints 4696 - a -33.5% break from the band, in the same week orders jumped by over 500. A real AOV collapse of a third in one week, with revenue roughly flat, would require a dramatic mix change that no one has reported; a build error - orders double-counted from a new source while revenue was not, or a partial revenue load against a full orders load - produces exactly this signature. The pack does not ship until the W11 orders figure is traced to its source rows. This is the sanity check's whole method: maintain a short list of derived ratios with known plausible bands (AOV, conversion, revenue per day), compute them at build time, and hold the pack when one leaves its band. The check cannot prove a figure right - a subtle error inside the band sails through - but it catches the loud errors, which are the ones that embarrass you in the meeting. Treat a held pack as the system working, and say so when you announce the delay.

This week's revenue is down 9% and the draft commentary blames the new pricing. Before that ships, run the standard investigation: is the drop broad, or concentrated? Daily revenue by channel is in a table.

The standing investigation order is: concentration first (channel, then day), data checks second, business causes last. Most 'business' drops that reach commentary are one channel or one day wearing a trench coat:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE channel_daily (day TEXT NOT NULL, channel TEXT NOT NULL, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT channel, SUM(CASE WHEN day = 'W11' THEN revenue_cents ELSE -revenue_cents END) AS change_cents FROM channel_daily GROUP BY channel ORDER BY change_cents
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN day = 'W11' THEN revenue_cents ELSE -revenue_cents END) AS total_change FROM channel_daily

Total change: -532000 cents. By channel:
channel | change_cents
phone | -432000
store | -50000
web | -50000
Phone accounts for 81.2% of the entire decline (-432000 of -532000); web and store are each down modestly and plausibly. A pricing change does not selectively amputate the phone channel in one week - but a phone-system outage, a changed number, a staffing gap, or a broken call-tracking feed does exactly this. The commentary blaming pricing was written from the headline alone, and it would have sent the pricing team into a week of defensive analysis while the phones quietly stayed broken. The investigation discipline is the pack's immune system: no causal claim ships in commentary until the drop has been localized by channel and by day, and the data-fault hypotheses (feed gaps, tracking changes) have been explicitly cleared. Concentration first is not bureaucracy - in this table it took one GROUP BY to redirect the entire company's attention from a strategy question to an operations incident.

Two sources feed our orders table and they disagree about last week: the platform says 1,048 orders, the warehouse system says 1,031. Both extracts are in tables. Reconcile them properly - I want the differing orders identified, not just the counts compared.

Count-level agreement proves nothing and count-level disagreement explains nothing. The reconciliation has to happen at the key level: which order IDs exist in one source and not the other, in both directions:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE platform_orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)
CREATE TABLE warehouse_orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)
SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(order_id) AS ids FROM platform_orders WHERE order_id NOT IN (SELECT order_id FROM warehouse_orders)
SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(order_id) AS ids FROM warehouse_orders WHERE order_id NOT IN (SELECT order_id FROM platform_orders)

messages.content: Key-level reconciliation of the sample extracts: orders 111,112 exist on the platform but not in the warehouse system; order 113 exists in the warehouse but not on the platform. Three distinct stories, and each has a different owner. Orders 111 and 112 are probably timing - placed late in the week, not yet picked - and will clear. Order 113 in the warehouse with no platform record is the interesting one: a manual or phone order entered directly into fulfillment, invisible to every platform-based report, which means the pack's order count and the warehouse's workload will never agree until that entry path is governed. This is why reconciliation is a key-level exercise: the count difference (12 versus 11 here; 1048 versus 1031 at full scale) is a symptom that cannot distinguish timing from leakage from double-counting, while the ID lists route each discrepancy to its cause in one step. The pack should carry the unreconciled count as a data-quality line until the manual-entry path is either integrated or formally accepted as a known gap with a named size.
The pack shows a 'data quality' line I want to formalize: the share of orders with a missing category, tracked weekly. Orders table has the category column. Compute the trend for the last four weeks.

The four checks run in a fixed order because each can invalidate the next one's evidence: freshness and gaps first (is the data complete?), ratio sanity second (is it plausible?), concentration last (where did it move?). The workspace holds daily sales, a freshness registry, and weekly orders:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE daily_sales (day TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE source_freshness (source TEXT PRIMARY KEY, latest_record_date TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE weekly_orders (week TEXT PRIMARY KEY, orders INTEGER NOT NULL, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO source_freshness VALUES ('sales', '2026-03-07'), ('orders', '2026-03-07')
INSERT INTO weekly_orders VALUES ('W09', 1055, 7385000), ('W10', 1048, 7404000)

The value of running the full pass on a clean week is not the verdict; it is that the verdict is earned by checks rather than by nobody having complained yet. Every figure in this verdict came from a query against the data itself, never from the build's scaffolding - that, too, is part of the discipline. Keep the four checks in fixed order, keep their outputs in the pack's appendix, and let 'all checks passed' be a claim with evidence behind it.

Monday's revenue in the daily table looks exactly double its usual size. The load log suggests Monday's file may have been loaded twice. Daily sales and a load log are here - prove it and tell me the corrected figure.
A double load is provable, not just plausible: the load log shows the file processed twice, and if the table has no deduplication the day's total is exactly twice the file's content. Both checks:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE daily_sales (day TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE load_log (file_name TEXT NOT NULL, loaded_at TEXT NOT NULL, rows_loaded INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_for_monday, SUM(amount_cents) AS loaded_total FROM daily_sales WHERE day = '2026-03-02'
SELECT COUNT(*) AS times_loaded FROM load_log WHERE file_name = 'sales_2026-03-02.csv'

messages.content: Proven. The load log shows Monday's file was processed 2 times, and the table holds 4 rows for Monday summing to 807000 cents - the file's two store rows, loaded twice. Monday's true revenue is the file's content: 403500 cents across its two store rows (214500 and 189000). The table's 807000 cents is exactly double that. Corrected Monday: 403500 cents, in line with Tuesday and Wednesday. The pack consequences, in order: any figure built on the doubled day (the weekly total, the week-over-week comparison, Monday's day-of-week average) is restated with a note; the load process gains an idempotency guard - a uniqueness check on file name in the load log, or a primary key that makes a second load fail loudly instead of succeeding silently; and the incident joins the data-quality log. A double load is the friendliest kind of corruption because it is exact and reversible, but only if it is caught before the doubled figure becomes someone's baseline.

One pack, three audiences: executives, operators, and analysts all read our weekly numbers. I have the week's core figures in a summary table. Show me how the three cuts differ while staying numerically identical.
Same source, three depths. The rule is that the figures may be framed differently but never recomputed differently - one query feeds all three versions, so a number cannot drift between audiences:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE week_summary (week TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, orders INTEGER NOT NULL, backlog INTEGER NOT NULL, sla_pct REAL NOT NULL)
SELECT week, revenue_cents, orders, backlog, sla_pct FROM week_summary ORDER BY week

W10 | 7404000 | 1048 | 380 | 91.5
W11 | 7692000 | 1091 | 402 | 90.8

Review my pack commentary draft against the data. Draft says: 'Customers are losing confidence as churn concerns mount.' The figures table has this month's signups, churned accounts, and support sentiment scores. Rewrite the commentary to state only what the data shows.
Commentary discipline is a reporting control: every sentence must be traceable to a figure, and inferences must be labeled as inferences. Here is what the data actually contains:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE month_figures (month TEXT PRIMARY KEY, signups INTEGER NOT NULL, churned INTEGER NOT NULL, accounts INTEGER NOT NULL, sentiment_avg REAL NOT NULL)
SELECT month, ROUND(churned * 100.0 / accounts, 2) AS churn_pct FROM month_figures ORDER BY month

messages.content: What the data shows: signups grew 5.6% (1240 to 1310). Churn was 0.6% of accounts in February and 0.63% in March - three more accounts on a larger base, a rate move of three hundredths of a point. Sentiment averaged 4.2, then 4.1. Nothing in this table measures 'confidence', and 'concerns mount' describes no figure in it. The rewritten commentary: 'Signups grew 5.6%. Churn was broadly flat at 0.63% of accounts (34 accounts). Sentiment was broadly flat at 4.1 of 5. No figure this month supports a confidence narrative in either direction.' Flat is a finding, and writing it plainly is what makes the pack credible when a month genuinely moves. The draft's failure is the common one: it narrates a mood and then the figures are expected to illustrate it. Reverse the workflow - figures first, sentences second, and any sentence that cannot point at its figure gets cut or labeled as a hypothesis with the test that would settle it ('if confidence were falling, we would expect trial starts to soften; they rose').

Readers keep asking the same questions in pack meetings and I want to turn them into standing sections. There is a question log table with the question and how many times it was asked. Show me how the log drives the pack's evolution.

A recurring question is a missing section wearing a disguise. The log turns meeting folklore into data: frequency decides what gets promoted into the pack, and the promotion gets documented so the pack's growth is deliberate:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE question_log (question TEXT PRIMARY KEY, times_asked INTEGER NOT NULL, first_asked TEXT NOT NULL, status TEXT NOT NULL)

Every promotion is minuted with its date, so the pack's table of contents has a changelog and nobody wonders why the document grows. And the loop closes: once a question becomes a section, it leaves the log - if readers keep asking it anyway, the section is failing at its job, which is a finding about the section, not the readers.

Retirement rule: a tile is cut when views are near zero AND no reader can name a decision it feeds; it is kept, however unfashionable, when a small audience uses it to decide something real. Publish the cut list in the pack before removing anything - retirement by announcement, not by disappearance - and archive the tile definitions so a future need can resurrect them honestly.

Our pack goes to the leadership channel every Monday. I want a distribution rule: which figures are stable enough to quote in the chat summary, and which must stay behind the full pack because they are provisional? Use the figures table with a status column.

Distribution is a data-quality surface: the chat summary is the most-quoted and least-contextualized artifact the pack produces, so only final figures belong in it. The status column makes the rule a query instead of a judgment call made under time pressure:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE pack_figures (figure TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value TEXT NOT NULL, status TEXT NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO pack_figures VALUES ('revenue_w11', '7692000 cents', 'final'), ('orders_w11', '1091', 'final'), ('cohort_retention_feb', '34.0%', 'provisional - cohort window open'), ('inventory_days', '23.4', 'provisional - feed stale'), ('sla_w11', '90.8%', 'final')

orders_w11 | 1091

Held back:

The two held figures fail for different reasons - one is a cohort metric whose measurement window is still open (it will move, and probably down, as late conversions land), the other rests on a stale feed. Both will be quoted out of context within the hour if they enter the chat, and the correction never travels as far as the original number. The rule generalizes: the wider the distribution, the more final the figure must be. Chat gets finals only; the full pack may carry provisionals with their status printed beside them; the analyst appendix may carry exploratory cuts labeled as such. This is not secrecy - the held figures are in the pack for anyone who opens it - it is sequencing: a number should meet its audience at the moment it can defend itself. Add the status column to the build, and the Monday argument about 'can we quote this yet' becomes a lookup.

I want the pack to carry a changelog - readers should be able to see what changed in the pack itself, not just in the business. There is a pack_changes table. Show me this quarter's changes and how they get presented.
A pack that changes silently trains readers to distrust comparisons with their memory of last week's pack. The changelog is a small table and a standing section:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE pack_changes (change_date TEXT NOT NULL, change TEXT NOT NULL, reason TEXT NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO pack_changes VALUES ('2026-01-12', 'Refund rate moved to definition v2', 'pre-dispatch refunds excluded'), ('2026-02-03', 'One-off revenue split added to revenue section', 'readers asked 6 times'), ('2026-02-24', 'Inventory tile suspended', 'feed unreliable, freshness failures'), ('2026-03-03', 'Cohort table moved to a two-week lag', 'immature cells were being misread')

Presented in the pack as a standing 'About this pack' section, newest first, one line each: what changed, when, and why. The changelog converts all of those from trust incidents into documentation. The front page of the pack fits five tiles. I have eight candidates with a decision-value score from the readership survey and a build-cost score. Choose the five by value per the table, and show me the ranking logic so it is defensible.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE tile_candidates (tile TEXT PRIMARY KEY, decision_value INTEGER NOT NULL, build_cost INTEGER NOT NULL)

Cut to the appendix: regional_split, vanity_sessions, office_leaderboard. Last week a provisional revenue figure from the pack got quoted to a client and then the final figure came in different. I have the provisional and final values in a table. Build the correction note and the rule that prevents a repeat.
The correction has to travel at least as far as the error did, in the same channel, with both figures named. Here is the size of the gap first:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE figure_versions (figure TEXT PRIMARY KEY, provisional_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, final_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, quoted_externally INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO figure_versions VALUES ('revenue_w10', 7560000, 7404000, 1)
SELECT provisional_cents, final_cents, provisional_cents - final_cents AS gap_cents FROM figure_versions WHERE figure = 'revenue_w10'

messages.content: The gap: provisional 7560000 cents, final 7404000 - the quoted figure overstated revenue by 156000 cents, 2.11%. The correction note, for the same channel the quote traveled in: 'Correction: the W10 revenue figure quoted on Monday (7560000 cents) was provisional. The final figure is 7404000 cents, 156000 lower, because the provisional build included a settlement file that was later reversed. The final figure is the one of record.' Three properties make a correction work: it names both numbers (a vague 'the figure was revised' lets every reader assume their version was right), it gives the cause in one clause, and it declares which figure is of record. The preventive rule is the distribution discipline from the figures table: provisional figures are watermarked in the pack itself - not in a footnote, on the tile - and the pack's terms, stated on its cover, are that watermarked figures are internal only. A client should never be able to quote your provisional number because they should never have seen it unwatermarked. Corrections handled this way cost a little pride and buy a reputation for exactness; corrections handled quietly cost the reputation.
Which sections of the pack email actually get opened? The analytics table has section-level open counts for the last four editions. Give me the readership picture by section.

Section-level opens tell you where the pack's value concentrates - and which sections are being produced for an audience of zero. Four editions is a small sample, so the read is directional, but the extremes are informative:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE section_opens (section TEXT PRIMARY KEY, opens_4_editions INTEGER NOT NULL, recipients INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO section_opens VALUES ('headline_summary', 388, 100), ('revenue_bridge', 301, 100), ('support_watch', 244, 100), ('funnel', 187, 100), ('cohorts', 88, 100), ('appendix_tables', 34, 100)
SELECT section, ROUND(opens_4_editions * 100.0 / (recipients * 4), 1) AS open_rate_pct FROM section_opens ORDER BY open_rate_pct DESC

The headline summary is opened by 97% of recipients per edition - it is the pack, for most readers. The bridge and support sections hold a real audience. Cohorts at 22% and the appendix at 8.5% are specialist territory: low, but not zero, and the appendix's job is to exist for verification rather than to be read cover to cover, so its low rate is not an indictment. The actionable finding is the gradient itself: effort should be allocated in roughly this order, with the headline summary getting the most editorial care because it is the only section most stakeholders will ever see - which also means a headline error is the most expensive error the pack can make, and the pre-ship checks should be weighted accordingly. One caution: opens measure attention, not value. A section can be opened weekly by many and used by none; pair this table with the decision-value survey before cutting anything, and treat the two together as the pack's readership evidence.

Final piece for the distribution section: the pack needs an as-of and definitions footer that generates itself from the registry and the freshness table, so it can never describe last month's pack. Assemble it from the tables.

A footer typed by hand describes the pack its author remembers. A generated footer describes the pack that was actually built - definitions in force, versions, and data-as-of per source, pulled at build time:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE kpi_definitions (kpi TEXT NOT NULL, version INTEGER NOT NULL, effective_from TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE source_freshness (source TEXT PRIMARY KEY, latest_record_date TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO kpi_definitions VALUES ('revenue', 3, '2025-01-01'), ('refund_rate', 1, '2025-07-01'), ('refund_rate', 2, '2026-01-01'), ('backlog', 1, '2025-01-01')
INSERT INTO source_freshness VALUES ('sales', '2026-03-08'), ('support', '2026-03-08'), ('inventory', '2026-03-05')
SELECT kpi, MAX(version) AS version_in_force FROM kpi_definitions GROUP BY kpi ORDER BY kpi
SELECT source, MIN(latest_record_date) AS oldest_data FROM source_freshness

messages.content: The generated footer reads: 'Definitions in force: backlog v1, refund_rate v2, revenue v3. Data as of: sales March 8, support March 8, inventory March 5. This pack's oldest source data is 2026-03-05 (inventory).' Every element came from a table at build time, so the footer cannot claim refund rate v1 while the tiles run v2, and cannot hide that the inventory section rests on March 5 data - the staleness is printed in the pack's own footer, where a reader will see it before citing the figure. This is the pack's contract with its readers in miniature: what the numbers mean (definitions and versions), and how fresh they are (as-of per source), stated on the document itself. Generate it, never type it. The one maintenance obligation is that the registry and freshness tables must themselves be current - a generated footer built on a stale registry is worse than a typed one, because it lies with machinery's confidence. The build's integrity suite should therefore include the registry's own freshness as its first check.

Our 'active user' KPI counts anyone who logged in. Product wants it to mean something stricter: performed a core action in the last 28 days. Users table has last login and last core action dates. Show both definitions on the same population.
Redefining the headline user metric changes every ratio built on it, so the two definitions run side by side first - the gap between them is the size of the restatement the company is signing up for:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE users (user_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, last_login TEXT NOT NULL, last_core_action TEXT)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS login_active FROM users WHERE julianday('2026-03-09') - julianday(last_login) <= 28
SELECT COUNT(*) AS core_active FROM users WHERE last_core_action IS NOT NULL AND julianday('2026-03-09') - julianday(last_core_action) <= 28

messages.content: On the same 10 users at March 9: the login definition counts 9 active; the core-action definition counts 6 - a 33.3% smaller user base, without a single user changing their behavior. Users 5 and 9 log in but have never performed a core action; user 4's last core action falls outside the window. The stricter definition is better - it measures use, not attendance - but adopting it is a series break, and the pack must handle it as one: the new definition gets a registry version and effective date, the old series is archived, and for one transition quarter both are published so the trend readers can be re-anchored. What must not happen is the quiet swap, where 'active users' falls by a third overnight and the commentary reaches for churn stories. Every downstream ratio - conversion, revenue per active user, support tickets per user - inherits the break, so the registry entry should list the dependent KPIs explicitly. A definition change is a small migration project, not an edit.

Gross margin for the pack: revenue and COGS by month are in a table, in cents. Two analysts got different margins for March because one used gross revenue and the other net of refunds. Compute both and settle which the pack uses.
Margin disagreements are usually denominator disagreements in disguise. Both versions from the same rows, then the settlement:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE monthly_pnl (month TEXT PRIMARY KEY, gross_revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, refunds_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, cogs_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO monthly_pnl VALUES ('2026-03', 5210000, 142000, 2870000)
SELECT gross_revenue_cents, refunds_cents, gross_revenue_cents - refunds_cents AS net_revenue_cents, cogs_cents FROM monthly_pnl

messages.content: March: on gross revenue the margin is 44.9%; on net revenue (5068000 cents after 142000 of refunds) it is 43.4%. The 1.5-point gap is entirely the refunds treatment. The net version is the honest one for the pack: refunds are revenue the business did not keep, and a margin computed on money returned to customers flatters the operation in exactly the months when quality problems spike refunds - the worse the month, the better the flattering version looks relative to the truth. That perverse property settles it. The definition record should read: 'gross margin = (net revenue - COGS) / net revenue; net revenue is gross revenue minus refunds in the month the refund is issued' - note the second choice hidden in there, refund timing (month of refund versus month of original sale), which matters for restatements and must also be written down. Two analysts disagreeing is never a people problem; it is the sound of a definition that has not been finished yet.

Our NPS-style 'promoter share' KPI: the survey table has scores 0-10 per response. The definition I inherited says promoters are 9-10, detractors 0-6, and the KPI is the difference of shares. Implement it exactly and show the components.
Composite scores should always be published with their components visible - a single difference hides whether it moved because promoters grew or detractors shrank. The components first:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE survey_responses (response_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, score INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS responses, SUM(CASE WHEN score >= 9 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS promoters, SUM(CASE WHEN score <= 6 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS detractors FROM survey_responses

messages.content: Components: 11 promoters and 4 detractors among 20 responses. Promoter share 55%, detractor share 20%, composite score 35. The pack should print all three numbers, always: a composite that rises from 35 to 40 because detractors fell is a service-recovery story; the same rise driven by promoters growing is an advocacy story, and the responses differ. Two definition details deserve registry entries here. The passives (7-8) count in the denominator but in neither share - that is the inherited definition and it is why the shares do not sum to 100. And the response base itself is a definition: these are responses, not customers - if unhappy customers answer at twice the rate of happy ones, the score measures the respondent pool, and the pack should carry the response count beside the score so a thin month (20 responses is thin) reads with appropriate humility. Composite scores compress; the pack's job is to keep the uncompressed version one glance away.

The support KPI 'first contact resolution' is gamed: agents close tickets quickly and customers reopen them. Tickets table has reopened flags and reopen windows. Redefine the KPI so the gaming shows, and run both versions.
A KPI that can be gamed will be, once it carries consequences. The honest definition counts a ticket resolved only if it stays closed - no reopen within 7 days. Both versions on the same tickets:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE tickets (ticket_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, closed INTEGER NOT NULL, reopened_within_7d INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(closed) AS closed_count, COUNT(*) AS total FROM tickets
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN closed = 1 AND reopened_within_7d = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS stayed_closed FROM tickets

messages.content: Naive first-contact resolution: 10 of 12 tickets closed = 83.3%. Honest version - closed and stayed closed for 7 days: 6 of 12 = 50%. Four of the ten 'resolutions' were reopenings waiting to happen. The redefinition does two things: it removes the incentive to close prematurely (a fast close that reopens now counts against the agent), and it surfaces a real operational fact the naive KPI was hiding - a reopen rate of 4 in 10 closures is a diagnosis problem in the support process, worth more than the KPI itself. Two implementation notes for the registry: the honest KPI publishes on a 7-day lag, because a ticket closed yesterday has not yet proven it stayed closed - the same maturity discipline as cohort metrics; and the reopen window is part of the definition (7 days here), since a 30-day window would catch more late reopens and read lower still. When you tighten a gamed KPI, expect the number to fall and announce that expectation in advance, or the team will read the fall as their performance collapsing rather than the ruler straightening.

Warehouse wants 'inventory days' in the pack - how many days current stock lasts at the current sales pace. Stock value and daily COGS are in a table, cents throughout. Define and compute it, including what happens in a week where COGS dips.

Inventory days is stock divided by the daily burn rate. The definition's soft spot is the burn window: a single day's COGS is noisy, so the registered version uses the trailing 7-day average - both shown here so the choice is visible:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE inventory_snapshot (item TEXT PRIMARY KEY, stock_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, cogs_last_7d_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, cogs_yesterday_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO inventory_snapshot VALUES ('all stock', 1645000, 492000, 51000)
SELECT stock_cents, cogs_last_7d_cents, cogs_yesterday_cents FROM inventory_snapshot

messages.content: Inventory days on the registered definition (trailing 7-day burn): stock of 1645000 cents against a daily burn of about 70286 cents gives 23.4 days of cover. On yesterday's COGS alone it would read 32.3 days - a calmer-looking number produced by one slow day, not by more stock or slower selling. That gap is why the window belongs in the definition: a buyer watching the 1-day version would see cover 'improve' after every quiet day and 'worsen' after every busy one, and would learn to ignore the metric within a month. The 7-day version still moves - a genuine sales surge shortens cover within the week, as it should - but it moves for business reasons. Pair the KPI with its natural companion in the pack: days of cover by category, because the aggregate can sit at a comfortable 23.4 while one fast line is three days from a stockout. Averages over stock hide the shelf that is actually empty.

The pack's second page is a deep dive that rotates: whichever headline KPI moved most gets the deep dive that week. This week's candidates are in a table with their moves and normal volatility bands. Implement the rotation rule.

The rotation rule keeps the deep dive honest: the biggest move relative to its own normal volatility wins, so a naturally jumpy metric does not monopolize the page and a quiet metric's rare lurch gets its week:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE kpi_moves (kpi TEXT PRIMARY KEY, move_pct REAL NOT NULL, typical_abs_move_pct REAL NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO kpi_moves VALUES ('revenue', 3.9, 3.0), ('sla_attainment', -2.8, 1.2), ('backlog', 5.8, 4.5), ('refund_rate', 0.4, 0.9)
SELECT kpi, move_pct, ROUND(ABS(move_pct) / typical_abs_move_pct, 2) AS surprise_ratio FROM kpi_moves ORDER BY surprise_ratio DESC

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
kpi | move_pct | surprise_ratio
sla_attainment | -2.8 | 2.33
revenue | 3.9 | 1.3
backlog | 5.8 | 1.29
refund_rate | 0.4 | 0.44

Deep-dive ranking by surprise ratio:
kpi | move_pct | surprise_ratio
sla_attainment | -2.8 | 2.33
revenue | 3.9 | 1.3
backlog | 5.8 | 1.29

SLA attainment wins the deep dive: its move of -2.8% is 2.33 times its typical move, the largest relative disturbance on the board - bigger in surprise terms than backlog's larger raw move (5.8% against a typical 4.5%). Refund rate barely moved relative to its own noise and correctly stays a headline line. This normalization is the same principle as the alert thresholds: judge a move against the metric's own variance, not against other metrics. The rotation rule should be printed in the pack ('deep dive: the KPI with the largest move relative to its typical volatility') so readers know the page is assigned by rule, not by whoever shouted loudest in the planning meeting - and so a team whose metric takes the page three weeks running gets the hint that their volatility itself has become the story.

Add a 'last week in one paragraph' box to the pack: it must be generated from the week's figures table, not hand-written, so it cannot drift from the tables. Figures for the week are in the summary table.
Generated prose is a constraint worth having: the paragraph can only say what the figures support, because its sentences are assembled from the same query results as the tables. The figures:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE week_summary (week TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, orders INTEGER NOT NULL, backlog INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT week, revenue_cents, orders, backlog FROM week_summary ORDER BY week

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
week | revenue_cents | orders | backlog
W10 | 7404000 | 1048 | 380
W11 | 7692000 | 1091 | 402

Generated paragraph for W11: 'Revenue was 7692000 cents, up 3.9% on the week, on 1091 orders (up 4.1%). The backlog grew from 380 to 402, the week's watch item.' Every clause is a figure from the table or a computed change - the paragraph cannot accidentally promise a cause, a confidence, or a trend the data does not contain, because it has no words available for them. That is both the strength and the limit of generated commentary: it will never speculate, and it will never notice anything either. The pack design that follows: generated text for the factual spine (what moved, by how much, what is being watched), human commentary in a separate, labeled box for interpretation - where a named person owns the judgment. Readers learn which box is which within two editions, and the factual spine stays clean even on weeks when the interpretation is contested. Never let the two boxes merge into one unattributed voice; that is how speculation acquires the costume of fact.

The pack compares this week to a four-week average as well as to last week, to damp noise. Weekly revenue for five weeks is in a table. Compute both comparisons for the current week and show when they disagree in sign.
Last-week comparisons are noisy; a trailing four-week average is a calmer baseline, but it lags real turns. Printing both, with their known failure modes, is the pack's compromise:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE weekly_revenue (week TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT ROUND(AVG(revenue_cents), 0) AS trailing_4wk_avg FROM weekly_revenue WHERE week IN ('W07', 'W08', 'W09', 'W10')

messages.content: W11 revenue 7210000 cents. Against last week: -2.6%. Against the trailing four-week average of 7207250 cents: +0.04%. The two comparisons disagree in sign, and both are telling the truth about different questions. Last week was the best week in the window, so W11 fell against it; the average says W11 is a perfectly ordinary week, marginally above the recent run of weeks. The pack commentary should read: 'a normal week following an exceptional one' - not a decline story. The failure modes to print beside the method: the average baseline lags genuine turns (a real collapse reads as 'slightly below average' for its first week), and the last-week baseline manufactures drama out of mean reversion. Using both, a reader can triangulate: a week that is down on last week AND down on the average AND the average itself is rolling over is a trend; a week down on only the first is weather. The pack's job is to make that triangulation take ten seconds.

Our pack build takes figures from three source tables with different period conventions: one is calendar weeks, one is Monday-Sunday operational weeks, one is a 4-4-5 retail calendar. I need a period map table so every figure in the pack refers to the same days. Design and demonstrate it.

Period misalignment is the deepest quiet bug in recurring reporting: three correct figures about three slightly different weeks, compared as if they were one. The cure is a period map - one canonical period, with each source's covering dates made explicit:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE period_map (pack_week TEXT NOT NULL, source TEXT NOT NULL, source_period TEXT NOT NULL, covers_from TEXT NOT NULL, covers_to TEXT NOT NULL)
SELECT source, source_period, covers_from, covers_to FROM period_map WHERE pack_week = '2026-W10' AND NOT (covers_from = '2026-03-02' AND covers_to = '2026-03-08')

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
source | source_period | covers_from | covers_to
inventory | retail P3W2 | 2026-03-01 | 2026-03-07

The map exposes one misalignment for pack week 2026-W10:
source | source_period | covers_from | covers_to
inventory | retail P3W2 | 2026-03-01 | 2026-03-07
The inventory source's retail-calendar week covers March 1-7, one day earlier than the pack's March 2-8 - so the inventory figure in this week's pack describes a window shifted by a day against the sales and support figures it sits beside. One day sounds trivial until a month-end or a promotion boundary falls in the seam, at which point the pack compares a sales week containing the promotion to an inventory week that excludes its first day. The map does not force the sources to change their calendars - retail calendars exist for good reasons - it makes the offsets explicit and queryable, so the build can either adjust (pull inventory by explicit dates for the pack window) or disclose ('inventory: retail week, Mar 1-7'). Every recurring pack should have this table, and adding a new source to the pack should require adding its row. Misalignment discovered by the map is clerical; misalignment discovered by a reader is a credibility event.

Close the weekly pack family with the hardest discipline: the pack must be produced even in the week the analyst is away. Document the build as a checklist generated from the pack's own metadata table - steps, sources, checks - so a substitute can run it.
A pack that depends on one person's memory is a single point of failure with a deadline. The metadata table turns the build into a procedure: ordered steps, each with its source and its verification:
