4 | Assemble bridges and movers | weekly tables | bridge effects sum to total change
5 | Generate footer and changelog | registry, freshness | versions match registry
6 | Distribute finals to chat, full pack to channel | pack figures | no provisional figures in chat
Each step names its source and the check that proves it happened correctly - a substitute does not need to know why the calendar-spine check exists, only that the pack is held if it fails. This is the same philosophy as the rest of the pack's machinery: definitions in a registry, freshness in a table, changes in a changelog, and now the build itself in a table, so the whole reporting system is inspectable data rather than one analyst's habits. The test of the checklist is empirical: the next time the analyst is away, the substitute runs it and the pack ships on time with its checks green - or the checklist gets a new step where it failed. Document the pack you actually build, keep the document in the same repository as the queries, and the Monday pack stops being a person and becomes a system.

Our fiscal year starts in February, but the pack software compares calendar quarters. I have monthly revenue with both calendar and fiscal quarter labels derivable from the month. Show the same three months under both quarterings so I can make the case.
A quarter is a grouping, and the grouping decides which months share a total - and therefore which comparisons the pack makes. February through April under both systems:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE monthly_revenue (month TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT 'calendar Q1 (Feb-Apr is split)' AS view, SUM(revenue_cents) AS feb_apr_total FROM monthly_revenue WHERE month IN ('2026-02', '2026-03', '2026-04')

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
view | feb_apr_total
calendar Q1 (Feb-Apr is split) | 16030000

arguments.sql: SELECT SUM(revenue_cents) AS fiscal_q1_total FROM monthly_revenue WHERE month IN ('2026-02', '2026-03', '2026-04')
SELECT revenue_cents FROM monthly_revenue WHERE month = '2026-05'

messages.content: February-April revenue totals 16030000 cents under either arithmetic - the sum does not change. What changes is everything around it: in the calendar view, February and March close out Q1 while April opens Q2, so the pack's 'Q1' contains a February the business considers the start of its year, and April gets compared against a January it has nothing in common with. In the fiscal view, February-April is Q1, one coherent season, compared next year against itself. The case for the fiscal quartering is not tidiness; it is that comparisons are only meaningful between periods the business experiences as units - its seasons, its promotional calendar, its budget year. The pack fix is a mapping table (month to fiscal period), owned by finance, versioned like a definition, because the day the fiscal year changes, every historical comparison must be restated or explicitly broken. A pack that cannot say which calendar it keeps will eventually report a quarter that nobody in the business recognizes.
Growth this year is flattered by an acquisition we made in June - the acquired unit's revenue is in the table with a flag. Split reported growth into organic and acquired so the board sees both.

Reported growth that includes an acquisition measures the checkbook as well as the business. The split is a standard bridge: total change, minus the acquired unit's contribution, equals the organic change on the like-for-like base:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE revenue_by_unit (period TEXT NOT NULL, unit TEXT NOT NULL, acquired INTEGER NOT NULL, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT period, revenue_cents FROM revenue_by_unit WHERE unit = 'core' ORDER BY period
SELECT SUM(revenue_cents) AS reported_2026h2 FROM revenue_by_unit WHERE period = '2026-H2'

messages.content: Reported growth for H2: 18.7% - 23500000 cents against 19800000. Organic growth: 5.6% - the core business grew from 19800000 to 20900000 cents, and the acquired unit contributed the remaining 2600000, which is most of the headline. Neither figure is the 'real' one in isolation: reported growth is what the bank sees, organic growth is what the operators did, and a board needs both to judge both. The pack rules this implies: the acquired unit is flagged in the data from its first day (a flag added later invites arguments about which revenue was 'really' acquired), the split is published for the first full year after acquisition, and after that year the unit folds into the base with a changelog note - otherwise the pack carries a permanent asterisk that stops meaning anything. Growth quality is a first-class reporting quantity; a single growth number that mixes buying and building will flatter whoever did the buying.

December always looks like our best month and January our worst, and every year someone proposes celebrating in December and panicking in January. Three years of December and January revenue are in a table. Give me the seasonal index treatment.

A seasonal index turns the calendar from an annual surprise into a known quantity: each month's typical ratio to the average month. With three years of the two problem months plus the annual totals, the pattern is computable:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE monthly_revenue (month TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT ROUND(AVG(revenue_cents), 0) AS dec_avg FROM monthly_revenue WHERE strftime('%m', month) = '12'
SELECT ROUND(AVG(revenue_cents), 0) AS jan_avg FROM monthly_revenue WHERE strftime('%m', month) = '01'

messages.content: Three-year averages: December NULL cents, January NULL - December runs about 1.6 times January, every year, on schedule. January 2026's 4610000 is not a collapse; it is the highest January in the three years shown, sitting exactly where the seasonal pattern puts it. The pack treatment: publish the seasonal index beside the raw figures for the strongly seasonal months ('January, index 0.78 of an average month'), and judge each month against its own history - January against Januarys - rather than against its neighbors. The deeper point is organizational: a seasonal pattern that has repeated three times is no longer information, it is scenery, and commentary that reacts to scenery ('demand fell sharply in January') spends the pack's credibility on the calendar. Save the alarm for the January that breaks its own pattern - that January will be real news, and it will only be visible to a pack that knows what a normal January looks like.
We report a rolling 12-month total for revenue in the annual pack section. Monthly table is here. Show me how the rolling total updates and why it hides turns longer than the monthly figures do.

The rolling 12-month total is a smoothing device: each month it drops the oldest month and adds the newest. Its virtue is that seasonality cancels; its vice is that a turn enters it diluted twelvefold:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE monthly_revenue (month TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(revenue_cents) AS rolling_12_to_feb FROM monthly_revenue WHERE month BETWEEN '2025-03' AND '2026-02'
SELECT SUM(revenue_cents) AS rolling_12_to_mar FROM monthly_revenue WHERE month BETWEEN '2025-04' AND '2026-03'

messages.content: Rolling 12 months to February: 62130000 cents. To March: 62580000 - a change of +450000. That change has an exact decomposition: March 2026 (5210000) entered and March 2025 (4760000) left, and the difference between the entering and leaving months is the whole movement. January 2026 was weak (4610000, the seasonal trough) and February strong, but the rolling total cannot tell you any of that - it reports the year's accumulated weather, not this month's. Use it for what it is good at: covenant-style measures, capacity planning, and any audience that needs the seasonal noise removed. Never use it as the pack's early-warning figure: a business that falls off a cliff in March moves its rolling total by one twelfth of the fall, and by the time the rolling figure confesses, the monthly figures have been shouting for a quarter. The pack prints both, labeled with their temperaments - the rolling total as the climate, the monthly as the weather - and commentary that confuses the two gets rewritten.

Last comparison problem: our 'month' for reporting is actually a 4-4-5 retail calendar, so 'March' in the pack is not March. I have the period map for the current retail year. Explain to the team what our pack periods actually are, with the current period's real dates.
A 4-4-5 calendar makes quarters exactly 13 weeks and years exactly 52 (or 53) weeks, at the price of periods that drift against the civil calendar. The map is the whole truth of it:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE retail_periods (period TEXT PRIMARY KEY, starts TEXT NOT NULL, ends TEXT NOT NULL, weeks INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT period, starts, ends, weeks FROM retail_periods WHERE period = 'P03'
SELECT SUM(weeks) AS q1_weeks FROM retail_periods WHERE period IN ('P01', 'P02', 'P03')

messages.content: The current pack period, P03, runs 2026-03-29 to 2026-05-02 - it starts in what the civil calendar calls March and ends in May, and it is 5 weeks long. The quarter P01-P03 is exactly 13 weeks. So when the pack says 'March', it means P02 (March 1-28 this year) and when it says the quarter grew, it compares two exact 13-week spans - which is the system's real virtue: every period comparison is between equal-length periods, and the trading-day adjustment problem mostly evaporates. The costs are the ones this team keeps tripping on: pack periods cannot be compared to civil-calendar figures from outside (the tax month, the landlord's month) without the map; a 53-week year arrives periodically and makes one year-over-year comparison span unequal lengths; and new joiners will read 'P03' as a month until someone shows them this table. Keep the map in the pack's appendix, print each period's real dates on its page, and the calendar stops being a source of quiet confusion.

A dashboard tile for 'active subscriptions' counts rows in the subscriptions table, but cancelled subscriptions stay in the table with a status. Subscriptions data is here. Quantify the tile's overstatement.
Counting rows is not counting the thing. The tile's definition error is visible the moment the table is grouped by the status the tile ignores:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE subscriptions (sub_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, status TEXT NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO subscriptions VALUES (1, 'active'), (2, 'active'), (3, 'cancelled'), (4, 'active'), (5, 'paused'), (6, 'active'), (7, 'cancelled'), (8, 'active'), (9, 'active'), (10, 'cancelled'), (11, 'active'), (12, 'paused')
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS subs FROM subscriptions GROUP BY status ORDER BY status
SELECT COUNT(*) AS tile_count FROM subscriptions

messages.content:
The tile reports 12. The table's truth:
status | subs
active | 7
cancelled | 3
paused | 2
Active subscriptions number 7; the tile overstates them by 71.4% because it counts cancelled (3) and paused (2) rows as active. This class of error - a status-blind count - grows silently: the table accumulates history, so the tile drifts further from reality every month while appearing to show healthy growth (the tile's 'growth' is partly the growth of the cancelled pile). It is also the easiest integrity check in the suite: for every count tile, the build recomputes the count from the definition's status filter and compares. The definition question the business must answer is whether 'paused' belongs in the KPI - a genuinely arguable point, which is exactly why it belongs in the registry and not in a tile query someone wrote in 2024. Whatever the answer, the tile, the registry, and the pack must say the same thing.

The conversion tile divides signups by visits, but the visits table counts sessions and the signups table counts people, and a tracking change last month inflated sessions. I have both tables by week. Show the contamination and the fix.
A ratio is only as honest as the compatibility of its two sides. When one side's measurement changes and the other's does not, the ratio reports the measurement change as a business change:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE weekly_funnel_counts (week TEXT PRIMARY KEY, sessions INTEGER NOT NULL, signups INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT week, ROUND(signups * 100.0 / sessions, 1) AS conv_pct FROM weekly_funnel_counts ORDER BY week

messages.content:
Conversion by week:
week | conv_pct
W08 | 15
W09 | 15
W10 | 11.7
W11 | 11.6
W08 and W09 sit at 15% and 15%. From W10 the rate 'falls' to 11.7% and 11.6% - in the same weeks sessions jump by roughly 30% while signups grow gently. Human behavior does not do that; instrumentation does. A session-counting change (a new analytics tag firing on more events, a bot-filter removal) inflated the denominator, and the tile dutifully reported a conversion collapse. The tell is in the levels, which is why the pack prints levels beside every rate: a rate move with a denominator discontinuity is a measurement event until proven otherwise. The fixes: the tracking change gets a registry-style annotation on the series with its date, the pre-change sessions are restated if the mapping is known (or the series is broken visibly if it is not), and the tile gains a guardrail - if either side of a ratio moves more than a set band in a week, the tile flags itself for review before the pack narrates a collapse that happened in a tag manager.

Two dashboards show different revenue for the same month: ours says 4,962,000 cents, finance's says 4,540,000. The difference is supposed to be timing - orders we count at order date, they count at ship date. Orders table has both dates. Verify the timing explanation exactly.
A timing explanation is only acceptable if it reconciles to the cent. The differing population is the orders whose order month and ship month differ - they should account for the entire gap:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_date TEXT NOT NULL, ship_date TEXT, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS by_order_date FROM orders WHERE strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) = '2026-03'
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS by_ship_date FROM orders WHERE strftime('%Y-%m', ship_date) = '2026-03'

SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) = '2026-03' AND strftime('%Y-%m', ship_date) <> '2026-03' THEN amount_cents ELSE 0 END) AS out, SUM(CASE WHEN strftime('%Y-%m', ship_date) = '2026-03' AND strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) <> '2026-03' THEN amount_cents ELSE 0 END) AS inn FROM orders

messages.content: By order date, March is 4962000 cents; by ship date, 4540000. The bridge explains the 422000-cent gap exactly: 670000 cents of March orders shipped in April (out of finance's March), and 248000 cents of February orders shipped in March (into it) - and the net of those two boundary populations is precisely the difference between the two dashboards. Timing explanation verified, to the cent. That last step is the one teams skip: 'it's just timing' gets asserted and accepted, and one month the gap is timing plus a real error hiding inside it, indistinguishable because nobody built the bridge. Make the bridge a standing artifact - the two boundary populations, in and out, printed monthly - and the timing claim becomes a checkable fact with a stable size. When the bridge's net stops matching the dashboards' difference, something other than timing has entered, and that is the month the bridge earns its existence.
The average basket tile uses AVG over order lines instead of over orders, I suspect. Orders and lines tables are here. Show the two averages and which one the business means.
AVG is grain-sensitive: averaging line values gives the average line, not the average basket, and small-basket orders get underweighted. Both computations on the same data:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)
CREATE TABLE order_lines (line_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_id INTEGER NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1), (2), (3), (4)
SELECT ROUND(AVG(amount_cents), 0) AS avg_line_cents FROM order_lines
SELECT ROUND(AVG(order_total), 0) AS avg_basket_cents FROM (SELECT order_id, SUM(amount_cents) AS order_total FROM order_lines GROUP BY order_id)

messages.content: Average line: 20000 cents. Average basket: 35000 cents. The tile has been reporting the line figure under the basket's name - a 15000-cent understatement of what a typical order is worth, because the four-line order and the one-line order count equally in the basket average but the line average lets big orders speak with more voices... in fact the reverse weighting: the line average weights every line equally, so the 60000-cent single-line order counts once while the three-line 30000-cent order counts three times at 10000. Any decision priced off 'average basket' - free-shipping thresholds, packaging, per-order cost allocations - has been priced off the wrong quantity. The general rule for the registry: every average's definition names its grain and its weighting ('mean of per-order totals, orders weighted equally'). An AVG without a stated grain is a defect waiting for a second table to expose it, and dashboards accumulate second tables the way harbors accumulate barnacles.

Capstone for dashboard integrity: run the full contract audit on our board - every tile traced to a definition, every definition's grain and filter checked against the tile's query metadata, stale tiles flagged. The metadata tables are in the workspace.

The audit joins three metadata tables: tiles (with their claimed definition, grain, and filter), the registry (current versions), and the refresh log (freshness). Every failure class from this family's history is one query:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE dashboard_tiles (tile TEXT PRIMARY KEY, kpi TEXT NOT NULL, claimed_version INTEGER NOT NULL, grain TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE kpi_definitions (kpi TEXT NOT NULL, version INTEGER NOT NULL, grain TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE tile_refresh_log (tile TEXT NOT NULL, refreshed_at TEXT NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO dashboard_tiles VALUES ('Revenue', 'revenue', 3, 'order'), ('Avg basket', 'avg_basket', 1, 'line'), ('Refund rate', 'refund_rate', 1, 'order'), ('Engagement', 'engagement_score', 1, 'user'), ('Backlog', 'backlog', 1, 'ticket')
INSERT INTO kpi_definitions VALUES ('revenue', 3, 'order'), ('avg_basket', 1, 'order'), ('refund_rate', 2, 'order'), ('backlog', 1, 'ticket')
INSERT INTO tile_refresh_log VALUES ('Revenue', '2026-03-09'), ('Avg basket', '2026-03-09'), ('Refund rate', '2026-03-09'), ('Engagement', '2026-03-09'), ('Backlog', '2026-03-02')
SELECT t.tile FROM dashboard_tiles t LEFT JOIN kpi_definitions d ON d.kpi = t.kpi WHERE d.kpi IS NULL

SELECT t.tile, t.grain AS tile_grain, d.grain AS registered_grain FROM dashboard_tiles t JOIN kpi_definitions d ON d.kpi = t.kpi AND d.version = (SELECT MAX(version) FROM kpi_definitions WHERE kpi = t.kpi) WHERE t.grain <> d.grain

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
tile | tile_grain | registered_grain
Avg basket | line | order

arguments.sql: SELECT t.tile, t.claimed_version, MAX(d.version) AS current_version FROM dashboard_tiles t JOIN kpi_definitions d ON d.kpi = t.kpi GROUP BY t.tile, t.claimed_version HAVING t.claimed_version <> MAX(d.version)
SELECT tile FROM tile_refresh_log GROUP BY tile HAVING CAST(julianday('2026-03-09') - julianday(MAX(refreshed_at)) AS INTEGER) > 1

messages.content: Contract audit findings, one of each failure class. Orphan: Engagement - no registered definition exists for its KPI. Grain violation: Avg basket runs at 'line' grain while its definition registers 'order' - the average-basket defect, caught by metadata instead of by a skeptical analyst. Version drift: Refund rate claims v1 against the registry's v2. Staleness: Backlog has not refreshed within the window. Only the Revenue tile passes clean. The audit's power is that it runs on metadata - it does not need to execute a single tile query, so it can run at every build, in milliseconds, and hold publication on any finding. This is the dashboard's contract made executable: definitions registered, tiles claiming versions and grains, freshness logged, and a join that refuses to let any of the three drift from the others unnoticed. A board maintained this way can still be wrong - the definitions themselves might be poor - but it cannot be silently wrong in the ways that actually happen.

One more cohort view for the pack: expansion revenue by cohort - how much existing cohorts grow or shrink their spend over time, separate from new-cohort acquisition. Cohort spend by quarter is in a table.
Total revenue growth mixes two engines: new cohorts arriving, and old cohorts expanding or contracting. Separating them tells you whether growth is bought or earned from the base:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE cohort_spend (cohort TEXT NOT NULL, quarter TEXT NOT NULL, spend_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO cohort_spend VALUES ('2025 cohort', 'Q4', 4200000), ('2025 cohort', 'Q1', 4530000), ('2026 cohort', 'Q1', 1180000)
SELECT spend_cents FROM cohort_spend WHERE cohort = '2025 cohort' AND quarter = 'Q4'

SELECT SUM(spend_cents) AS q1_total, SUM(CASE WHEN cohort = '2025 cohort' THEN spend_cents END) AS from_2025, SUM(CASE WHEN cohort = '2026 cohort' THEN spend_cents END) AS from_2026 FROM cohort_spend WHERE quarter = 'Q1'

messages.content: Q1 total: 5710000 cents. Of it, 4530000 came from the 2025 cohort - which grew 7.9% over its own Q4 spend of 4200000 - and 1180000 came from the new 2026 cohort. So Q1's growth over Q4 decomposes into base expansion of 330000 cents plus new-cohort acquisition of 1180000: the quarter's growth was mostly bought with new logos, while the base quietly expanded at a healthy 7.9%. Both facts matter and they pull in different directions - acquisition-led growth needs the acquisition engine to keep running; base expansion compounds on its own. The metric to watch in future quarters is the expansion rate's sign: the quarter the existing base contracts (negative expansion, sometimes called churn drag in revenue terms) the business must acquire just to stand still, and that is a strategic alarm the totals will hide for quarters. The cohort spend table is three rows here; in the real pack it is the full triangle, and this decomposition is computed on it every quarter as a matter of routine.

Retention curves: two monthly cohorts' retained users at months 1, 2, and 3 are in a table. Compare the curves properly - same ages - and quantify which cohort is better and by how much at month 3, accounting for their different sizes.
Curves are compared at equal ages, and the comparison should be in rates with sizes attached, because a rate gap on a small cohort is a weaker claim than the same gap on a large one:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE cohort_retention (cohort TEXT NOT NULL, cohort_size INTEGER NOT NULL, month_since INTEGER NOT NULL, retained INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT cohort, month_since, retained, ROUND(retained * 100.0 / cohort_size, 1) AS retained_pct FROM cohort_retention ORDER BY month_since, cohort

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
cohort | month_since | retained | retained_pct
Feb | 1 | 930 | 62
Jan | 1 | 780 | 65
Feb | 2 | 765 | 51
Jan | 2 | 660 | 55
Feb | 3 | 660 | 44
Jan | 3 | 588 | 49

The curves at equal ages:
cohort | month_since | retained | retained_pct
Feb | 1 | 930 | 62
Jan | 1 | 780 | 65
Feb | 2 | 765 | 51
Jan | 2 | 660 | 55
Feb | 3 | 660 | 44
Jan | 3 | 588 | 49
January runs 65.0%, 55.0%, 49% at months 1-3; February runs 62.0%, 51.0%, 44%. February is worse at every age, and at month 3 the gap is 5 points - on cohorts of 1200 and 1500, that gap represents roughly 75 users of difference at equal size, well beyond a rounding artifact. February's curve is not just lower; its shape decays faster between months 1 and 2 (11 points against January's 10), suggesting the weakness is in early life - onboarding or expectation-setting - rather than in long-term fit. That shape reading is the value of the curve over a single retention number: a single month-3 figure would locate the problem in time (by month 3) but the curve locates it in the lifecycle (the first 60 days). The pack should print both cohorts' curves with sizes, and retire each cohort's curve from the chart once it is old enough to be history rather than signal - a chart with twelve curves teaches nothing; the discipline is comparing the newest against the best and the typical.

The funnel section needs a data-quality guard: stage counts should be monotonically non-increasing for a gated funnel, and the build should flag violations. This week's stage counts are in a table. Run the monotonicity check.

For a truly gated funnel - every paid user passed trial, every trial passed signup - counts must never increase down the stages. A violation is never a business insight; it is a measurement defect with an address:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE funnel_stages (stage_order INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, stage TEXT NOT NULL, users INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO funnel_stages VALUES (1, 'visit', 22500), (2, 'signup', 3300), (3, 'trial', 1720), (4, 'paid', 1745)

SELECT a.stage AS earlier_stage, b.stage AS later_stage, a.users AS earlier_users, b.users AS later_users FROM funnel_stages a JOIN funnel_stages b ON b.stage_order = a.stage_order + 1 WHERE b.users > a.users

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
earlier_stage | later_stage | earlier_users | later_users
trial | paid | 1720 | 1745

One violation: paid (1745 users) exceeds trial (1720) - 25 more paid than trial, which is impossible in a gated funnel. The count cannot be a real surplus of customers; it is one of the known defects: a path that reaches paid without a trial event (a reseller or migration flow), duplicate paid events, or a trial event lost to a tracking gap. The build's job is to flag it and hold the funnel section - publishing a conversion rate above 100% for that stage, or quietly capping it, both teach readers the funnel is decorative. The investigation routes by the drill: split the stages by source and the violating path usually identifies itself in one query. And the check itself belongs in the integrity suite permanently, stated as an invariant in the funnel's definition record: 'for the gated product path, stage counts are non-increasing; violations indicate instrumentation or an ungated path, and are reported, never smoothed.' A funnel that can violate its own geometry without comment is not a funnel; it is four unrelated numbers in a trench coat.

Anomaly follow-up: last month's spike investigation concluded the partner feed had replayed a batch. I need the corrected signup series - the table has a duplicate flag from the dedupe process. Produce the corrected counts and the restatement note.

The correction is a restatement, handled like the revenue one: corrected figures published, the size of the correction named, the original figures kept on record. The dedupe flags make the corrected series a query:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE signups (signup_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, day TEXT NOT NULL, source TEXT NOT NULL, is_duplicate INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS reported, SUM(CASE WHEN is_duplicate = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS corrected FROM signups GROUP BY day ORDER BY day
SELECT COUNT(*) AS duplicate_rows FROM signups WHERE is_duplicate = 1

messages.content:
Corrected series:
day | reported | corrected
2026-03-02 | 3 | 3
2026-03-03 | 9 | 4
2026-03-04 | 3 | 3
Tuesday March 3 was reported as 9 signups; the corrected figure is 4, after removing 5 replayed partner rows. Monday and Wednesday are untouched. The restatement note for the pack: 'March 3 signups restated from 9 to 4: a partner feed replayed a batch of 5 records (the day's 2 genuine partner signups stand). All downstream figures for that week - signup totals, activation denominators - are restated on the same basis.' Note what the correction does to the earlier investigation's open question: the spike was a fault, not an event, and the partner's genuine Tuesday contribution was unremarkable. Two process items close the incident: the feed gains an idempotency key so a replay is rejected at load, and the spike drill (concentration by source) that caught this becomes a standing build check on any day whose signups move beyond the alert band. Incidents that end with a standing check are tuition; incidents that end with a corrected number and nothing else are subscriptions.

Threshold question for the watch section: at what backlog level should the pack escalate from 'watch' to 'problem'? I have a year of weekly backlog values and the weeks where the team actually had to intervene. Derive the threshold from that history.

An escalation threshold should be learned from the operation's own history: the level above which intervention became necessary, not a round number someone picked. The history separates into intervened and not-intervened weeks:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE backlog_history (week TEXT PRIMARY KEY, backlog INTEGER NOT NULL, intervened INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT MAX(CASE WHEN intervened = 0 THEN backlog END) AS highest_no_intervention, MIN(CASE WHEN intervened = 1 THEN backlog END) AS lowest_intervention FROM backlog_history

messages.content: The history separates almost cleanly: the highest backlog week that needed no intervention is 371; the lowest week that did need one is 381. The overlap band between them - roughly 371 to 381 - is where judgment lives, and the escalation threshold belongs at its top: escalate at 385, say, just above the lowest intervention, and the pack will escalate slightly late once in a while rather than crying wolf at levels the team has repeatedly absorbed. One intervened week sits below the band (381's intervention and 388's are the joint-lowest region), which is honest noise - interventions also happen for reasons backlog size does not capture, like a holiday week shrinking capacity. The method is the point: thresholds derived from the operation's own intervention history, reviewed quarterly as new history accrues, and recorded in the registry with their derivation ('set March 2026 from 12 weeks of history: lowest intervention 381'). A threshold with a derivation can be defended and improved; a threshold that is a round number can only be obeyed or ignored, and ignored is where round numbers end up.

We now send the pack to a second region whose week runs Sunday to Saturday while ours runs Monday to Sunday. Leadership wants one pack, not two. I have the daily sales table. Show me what changes and what must not.

The figures must not change their meaning, but the windowing genuinely differs by region - so the honest design is one build, two windowings, with the difference disclosed and quantified rather than averaged away:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE daily_sales (day TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT SUM(revenue_cents) AS mon_sun_week FROM daily_sales WHERE day BETWEEN '2026-03-02' AND '2026-03-08'
SELECT SUM(revenue_cents) AS sun_sat_week FROM daily_sales WHERE day BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-07'

messages.content: The same business, two honest weeks: Monday-Sunday totals 2872000 cents; Sunday-Saturday totals 2860000. The 12000-cent difference is exactly the boundary swap - Sunday March 1 (298000) enters one window as Sunday March 8 (310000) leaves it. Nothing is wrong, and that is precisely why it is dangerous: two regions comparing 'this week's revenue' in a joint meeting will disagree by a boundary day and, if the windowing is not printed on the pack, will burn the meeting on a phantom discrepancy. The design: the pack carries both windowings for the shared headline figures, each labeled with its dates (never just 'week of'), regional sections use the local window, and group-level commentary uses one declared group window. What must not happen is the quiet compromise - a single 'global week' imposed on both - because then one region's pack stops matching the week its own operation actually lived. Distribution across regions is a windowing problem, and windowing problems are solved by printing the dates, every time.

No single week looks wrong, but the quarter's revenue per the pack is slightly less than the sum of the daily table - a slow leak. Weekly published figures and the daily table are here. Quantify the leak and characterize it.

Slow leaks are invisible to per-week checks because each week's gap is inside the noise band. The detection is cumulative: compare the published series against the raw grain over the whole quarter and look at the gap's pattern, not its size in any one week:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE daily_sales (day TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE published_weekly (week TEXT PRIMARY KEY, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO published_weekly VALUES ('W10', 2037000), ('W11', 2071000)
SELECT strftime('%Y-W%W', day) AS wk, SUM(revenue_cents) AS raw_total FROM daily_sales GROUP BY wk ORDER BY wk

messages.content:
Raw weekly totals from the daily grain:
wk | raw_total
2026-W09 | 2042000
2026-W10 | 2076000
Published for the same two weeks: 2037000 and 2071000. Each week is short by exactly 5000 cents - a leak of 10000 cents over the two weeks, and the pattern is the diagnosis: a constant gap, not a proportional one. A percentage-shaped gap would suggest a filter excluding a category; a constant 5000 every week suggests a fixed item being dropped - one store's fixed daily report of 1000 cents across 5 days, or a standing adjustment applied in the build and never documented. Constant leaks are found by differencing the series, never by inspecting either series alone, because both look plausible in isolation. The pack consequence: the quarterly self-audit (published versus raw, differenced week by week) is the only check shaped to catch this, which is why it runs on a calendar rather than on suspicion. And once found, the gap is not plugged with a correction factor - the dropped item is identified and restored at the source, because a build that adds back 5000 a week has learned to hide a symptom at exactly the rate it occurs.

Capstone: walk me through a definition change done right, end to end. We are tightening 'active user' next month. Use the registry and a restatement of last quarter's headline figures - old definition in the published table, new definition computable from the users table.

Version 2 takes effect April 1 and is a new row, not an edit - version 1's definition remains queryable forever, so any historical figure can be interpreted. The break, quantified from the dual-run on the current population (9 login-active against 6 core-active in the sample), scales as follows: March's published figure of 5490 under version 1 restates to approximately 3660 under version 2's stricter rule; the exact restatement is computed user-by-user in the real build, and the ratio here is the planning estimate. Every element of this protocol exists because some team, somewhere, skipped it and spent a quarter arguing about a ruler change as if it were a business event. The definition change is the easiest kind of reporting crisis to prevent, because it is the only one you schedule yourself.

The reporting system deserves the same treatment it gives the business: defined metrics, computed from its own records, with the uncomfortable ones included. Four small tables hold its history:

messages.content: Reporting system health, Q1. Registry: 6 KPIs registered across 8 definition versions - the version count matters, because it shows definitions are being maintained, not just created. Contract: 1 of 7 tiles is an orphan (the engagement tile, still awaiting its definition - it goes on the quarter's fix list, again, and this time with an owner). Restatements: 3 months restated, average size 0.67% - small and shrinking, the signature of late data being handled honestly rather than of instability. Alerts: 4 fired, 2 mattered - a 50% hit rate, up from the era when a third of weeks alerted and almost none mattered. This is the pack turned on itself, and it belongs in the quarterly review for the same reason the business figures belong in the weekly pack: a system that reports on everything except its own reliability is asking for trust it has not earned. The four numbers together are the reporting system's KPI set - coverage, contract compliance, correction load, and alert precision - and they get definitions, thresholds, and an owner, like everything else in the registry.
